en: The Perfection of Wisdom in Eighteen Thousand Lines,
Chapter 70 (continued) – 82 /// [leaf broken off here]
VI. Abhisamaya (VIa) Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [seeks] unsurpassed perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena whose intrinsic nature is non-existence..."

He awakens to it. Therefore, Blessed One, since all phenomena have the nature of non-existence, how is the gradual action of a bodhisattva mahāsattva discerned, and how are his gradual training and gradual practice discerned—
by means of which gradual action, gradual training, and gradual practice he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva has previously heard thus from the presence of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
or from the presence of arhats who have attended upon bodhisattva mahāsattvas regarding the qualities of a Buddha."

Whether it be non-returners (*anāgāmin*), or once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or stream-enterers (*srotaāpanna*); the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvatva*) belongs to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;

the nature of non-existence belongs to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas; the nature of non-existence belongs to the Pratyekabuddhas; the nature of non-existence belongs to the Arhats; the nature of non-existence belongs to the non-returners; and the nature of non-existence belongs to the stream-enterers.
The nature of non-existence belongs to all noble ones (*ārya*). There is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), not even so much as the tip of a blade of grass.
Furthermore, it occurs to that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: [as follows].
"Up to the level of the stream-enterers,
whether I shall realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment or shall not realize it,

all phenomena are indeed non-existent. Therefore, having realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, I shall lead those beings who dwell in the perception of existence to [the realization of] non-existence."
Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who would thus establish them indeed stands firm for unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment in order to bring about the final nirvāṇa of all sentient beings; he undertakes the gradual action, the gradual training, and the gradual practice.
Having trained therein, the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas of former times fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

From the very beginning, he practices the six perfections, namely: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
While practicing the perfection of generosity, he himself gives gifts and establishes others in the perfection of generosity.
He speaks in praise of generosity, and he also becomes a speaker of praise and a supporter of those others who practice the perfection of generosity.
Through that generosity, he obtains a great mass of wealth. He relinquishes gifts and gives gifts with a mind free from stinginess.
With a mind [of generosity], food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink...
To those who desire fragrance, he gives fragrance; to those who desire garlands, garlands; to those who desire ointments, ointments; to those who desire bedding, bedding.
By that very act of giving, he protects the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*). He attains both the majesty of the gods and the majesty of humans.
He attains the aggregate of ethical discipline, he attains the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhiskandha*), and he attains the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*).

He attains the aggregate of liberation; he attains the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. Endowed with that very generosity, he transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
having transcended the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he enters the bodhisattva’s certainty. The bodhisattva’s certainty...

Having entered [the path], purified the buddha-field, and ripened sentient beings, one attains all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Having attained all-aspect omniscience, one turns the wheel of Dharma;
having turned the wheel of Dharma, one establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles. What of that?
He liberates them from saṃsāra. In this way, Subhūti, the gradual action of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is discerned through giving;
his gradual training and gradual practice are discerned. Yet all that is not apprehended. Why is that?
Because it has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

Furthermore, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), establishes others in the perfection of ethical discipline,
speaks in praise of ethical discipline,
and both commends and approves of those others who practice the perfection of ethical discipline. By that...

Through ethical discipline, one attains greatness among gods and greatness among humans. By means of that ethical discipline, one establishes sentient beings in ethical discipline, establishes them in meditative concentration, establishes them in wisdom, establishes them in liberation, and establishes them in the knowledge and vision of liberation. One is endowed with that ethical discipline.

He transcends the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; having transcended the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, by means of that very aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he establishes beings in the three vehicles and liberates them from cyclic existence. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a Bodhisattva...
Through the ethical discipline of the Mahāsattva, gradual action is discerned; gradual training and gradual practice are discerned;
yet all that is not apprehended. Why is that?
Because it has no intrinsic nature.

(VI 3) Furthermore, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience himself; he speaks in praise of patience to others and encourages others to practice the perfection of patience.
He also speaks in praise of those who practice the perfection of patience and approves of them. He [practices] the perfection of patience...
He establishes them in ethical discipline, he establishes them in meditative concentration, he establishes them in wisdom, he establishes them in liberation,

and he establishes them in the knowledge and vision of liberation. By means of that aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—

By means of the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva; having established sentient beings in the three vehicles, he liberates them from cyclic existence.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that the gradual practice of patience by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is recognized. That...
And all that is not apprehended. For what reason?
Because it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, Subhūti...
Regarding wholesome qualities, they encourage others to undertake vigor, speak in praise of vigor,
and both commend and approve of others who exert vigor.
They establish them in ethical discipline, establish them in concentration, establish them in wisdom, and [establish them] in liberation.

He establishes them. He establishes them in the knowledge and vision of liberation; and by means of the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, having transcended the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he [establishes them] by that very same aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, and aggregate of liberation.

By means of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, having established beings in the three vehicles, he liberates them from cyclic existence. It is in this way, Subhūti, that the gradual action of a bodhisattva mahāsattva through diligence is known; his gradual training and gradual practice are known. And yet, he does not apprehend any of that.
For what reason?
Because it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) by himself...

He establishes them in the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). He speaks in praise of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

He also speaks in praise [of it] and approves of it. Having established himself there in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and having established himself in the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), he establishes others in ethical discipline (*śīla*), establishes them in concentration (*samādhi*), and establishes them in wisdom (*prajñā*). He establishes them in liberation (*vimukti*), and establishes them in the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*). By means of that aggregate of ethical discipline and that aggregate of concentration...

Having transcended the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas by means of the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation— and likewise by means of that very same aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation,
and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—
In this way, Subhūti, the gradual practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva through meditative concentration is discerned, yet all of that is not apprehended. Why is that?
Because it has no intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening onward, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom establishes beings in generosity; he establishes them in ethical discipline; he establishes them in meditative concentration;
he establishes them in wisdom; he establishes them in liberation; and he establishes them in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
For one who courses in the perfection of wisdom by oneself...

He accomplishes patience. He exerts vigor. He establishes himself in meditative concentration. He speaks in praise of generosity; he speaks in praise of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentrations, and wisdom. He is one who speaks in praise of others who cultivate these as well, and he approves of them. Through that perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline...
By means of the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom, one transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

having transcended the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva. Having purified the buddha-field and matured sentient beings, one attains the knowledge of all aspects. Having established sentient beings in the three vehicles, [one attains that state].
He liberates [beings] from cyclic existence, yet he does not apprehend any of that. Why is that? Because it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva performs the gradual practice...

He trains in the gradual training and the gradual setting forth. Beginning from the first production of the thought of awakening, he resolves that all phenomena have the nature of non-existence by means of mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects. He cultivates the recollection of the Buddha;

he cultivates the recollection of the Dharma; he cultivates the recollection of the Saṅgha; he cultivates the recollection of ethical discipline, the recollection of generosity, and the recollection of the deities.
(VI 7) And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of the Buddha?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attend to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, by way of form. Nor by way of feeling.
Why is that?
For thus, form has no intrinsic nature;
that which has no intrinsic nature is a non-entity.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no intrinsic nature; that which has no intrinsic nature is a non-entity. Why is that?
For non-recollection and non-mental attention are indeed the recollection of the Buddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not to be mentally attended to by means of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, nor by his golden complexion.
One should attend to it by way of the body.
Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the body, its radiance, and its secondary marks does not exist; that which has no intrinsic nature is a non-entity. Why is that?
For non-recollection and non-mental engagement are indeed the recollection of the Buddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not to be mentally engaged with by way of the aggregate of ethical discipline,
nor by way of the aggregate of concentration, nor by way of the aggregate of wisdom, nor by way of the aggregate of liberation, nor by way of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
It should be brought to mind. Why is that?

Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation does not exist; that which has no intrinsic nature is a non-entity (*abhāva*). Why is that?
For non-recollection and non-mental engagement is indeed the recollection of the Buddha.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not to be mentally engaged by means of the ten powers of a Tathāgata; nor by the four grounds of self-confidence, nor by the four analytical knowledges, nor by great loving-kindness.
One should not attend to it by means of great compassion, nor by means of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Why is that?
Because they have no intrinsic nature; that which has no intrinsic nature is a non-entity. Why is that?
For the recollection of the Buddha consists in non-recollection and non-mental-attention.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not to be brought to mind by way of dependent origination. Why is that?
Because he has no intrinsic nature; that which has no intrinsic nature is a non-entity. Why is that?
For the recollection of the Buddha consists in non-recollection and non-mental engagement.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should bring to mind the recollection of the Buddhas. In this way, indeed, his gradual action, gradual training, and gradual setting forth are made known;
training in this gradual action, gradual training, and gradual setting forth, he fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness through those gradual settings forth.

Through the yoga of the nature of non-existence, he fulfills the abandonments, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the noble eightfold path, up to the flood of the knowledge of all aspects. He perfectly awakens to all phenomena as being precisely non-existent—wherein even the notion of intrinsic nature does not exist. (VI 8) And how, Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of the Dharma?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not attend to wholesome dharmas, nor should they attend to unwholesome dharmas; nor to those that are predicted [to enlightenment], nor to those that are not predicted; nor to worldly dharmas, nor to supramundane dharmas; nor to those with material gain, nor to those without material gain; nor to noble dharmas, nor to ignoble dharmas; nor to dharmas with outflows, nor to dharmas without outflows; nor to those included within the desire realm.
They are not included within the realm of form, nor are they included within the formless realm.

For indeed, those phenomena have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); that which has no intrinsic nature is a non-entity (*abhāva*). Non-attention through the mindfulness of non-existence is indeed the recollection of phenomena (*dharmānusmṛti*). Herein, one awakens to phenomena where there is neither the notion of intrinsic nature nor even the notion of existence. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates the recollection of phenomena. And how, Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of the Saṅgha?
In this regard, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
The four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals, who are endowed with liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation—for what reason is this so?
It should be understood in this same way. For what reason?
Because it has no intrinsic nature; it is non-existence. Indeed, the recollection of the Saṅgha consists in non-recollection and non-mental engagement.
One attains it through non-recollection and non-mental engagement. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the recollection of the Saṅgha.
(VI 10) And how, Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*)?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), beginning from the first production of the thought of awakening...

One who is endowed with the ethical conduct that leads to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) should attend to those precepts as being of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva*), wherein there is not even the activity of mindfulness, let alone the absence of mindfulness. Why is that?
Because therein even the perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvasaṃjñā*) does not exist.
(VI 11) And how, Subhūti, should the recollection of relinquishment be cultivated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom?

Whether it be the renunciation of worldly gain or the renunciation of merit, one should not even give rise to the thought of "renouncing" in such cases—whether thinking, "I am giving" or "I am not giving," or "I am renouncing" or "I am not renouncing.
Why is that?
Because they have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus practicing and training in the recollection of relinquishment, he gradually attains even the knowledge of all aspects.
(VI 12) And how, Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivate the recollection of the deities?

Those who have been reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings, up to those reborn among the gods who wield power over the creations of others, should be contemplated as being of the nature of non-existence.

One should attend to those deities. Even where there is no activity of mindfulness, one who attends in this manner proceeds by stages until they attend to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
[Or rather, the formless realms and pride?
Those non-returners are to be attended to as being non-existent. For what reason?
Because they have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Those things which have no intrinsic nature are non-existent.
Even where there is no further activity of mindfulness, he, reflecting in this manner, gradually attends to everything up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
As he continues to reflect, his gradual action becomes manifest, his gradual training becomes manifest, and his gradual setting forth becomes manifest.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should,
by way of the yoga of the nature of non-existence, train in internal emptiness through gradual action, gradual training, and gradual setting forth.
One should train in great compassion. And while training in the path to enlightenment, one will fully awaken to dharmas that have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.
"In this way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, a gradual action is discerned; a gradual training and a gradual setting forth are discerned.
Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, then there is no form, and so on up to no consciousness; there are no aggregates, no elements, and no [sense-fields]."
"There is no affliction, there is no purification, there is no attainment, nor is there any realization, up to and including all phenomena.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, in phenomena whose intrinsic nature is non-existence, is either existence or non-existence apprehended?"
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One; for within all dharmas, which have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, neither existence nor non-existence is apprehended.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, Subhūti, how does this occur for you, Subhūti:

'If all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, then there is no form, up to and including no consciousness; there is no attainment, nor even no clear realization; and there is no such thing as all phenomena'? He replied: "O Blessed One, I have no doubt and no hesitation regarding these phenomena. Nevertheless, however..."

"Blessed One, in the future time there will be monks belonging to the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayānika*), or the vehicle of the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddhayānika*), or the vehicle of the bodhisattvas (*bodhisattvayānika*). They will speak thus: 'If all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāva*), then among all phenomena that have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, who here is afflicted or who is purified?'"

Not understanding affliction and purification, they will be corrupted in morality, corrupted in view, and corrupted in conduct. For those who are corrupted in morality, corrupted in view, and corrupted in conduct, one of three destinies is to be expected: either the realm of hell, the animal realm, or the world of Yama.

“Blessed One, seeing this future peril as well, I ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about this matter. Nevertheless, Blessed One, I have no doubt and no hesitation regarding these teachings.
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is just as you say.
Chapter 7. Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

“Blessed One, if all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, seeing what purpose does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that he establishes himself for the sake of beings in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?
The Blessed One replied:

Subhūti, just as all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, in that very same way the bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes himself for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For what reason?
Subhūti, [any other] apprehension is merely trivial.
For one who perceives through apprehension, there is no attainment, no clear realization, and no unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
He asked: "But, Blessed One, is there for non-apprehension an attainment, or a clear realization, or an unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
The Blessed One replied:

Subhūti, non-apprehension itself is attainment; non-apprehension is realization; non-apprehension itself is unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, by virtue of the non-disturbance of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Whoever would desire the attainment of non-apprehension, or its realization, or unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, would desire to disturb the realm of phenomena.
He said: "If, Blessed One, for that which is non-apprehension there is neither attainment nor clear realization nor unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—

if non-apprehension itself is attainment, non-apprehension itself is clear realization, and non-apprehension itself is unsurpassed perfect enlightenment— then, Blessed One, from where could there be a first stage for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"

From where does the second [ground] come? From where the third? From where up to the tenth ground? From where does the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) come?

From where do the superknowledges resulting from maturation (*vipākaja-abhijñā*) come? From where does the gift resulting from maturation come? From where does the ethical discipline resulting from maturation come? From where does the patience resulting from maturation come? From where does the vigor resulting from maturation come? From where does the meditative concentration resulting from maturation come? From where does the wisdom resulting from maturation come?

Abiding therein, he brings sentient beings to maturity through phenomena that are the result of maturation (*vipākīya*). He purifies a Buddha-field and attends upon the Blessed Buddhas with food, drink, clothing, perfumes, garlands, bedding, seats, dwellings, and the necessities of life, including various human prosperities; and these are never cut off from him.
It continues until, having brought about its maturation within the relics and the disciples of the one who has entered final nirvāṇa, it is not exhausted.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, it is precisely because there is no apprehension that there is the first ground, up to and including the tenth ground; it is for that very reason."
The five superknowledges are results of maturation; from that very [source], there is giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom that are results of maturation.

From that very [source] arise the roots of merit which are results of maturation, by means of which one performs the welfare of sentient beings, even up to making offerings after [the Buddha] has entered final nirvāṇa.
[They] proceed.

He asked: "O Blessed One, what is the distinction, what is the difference between non-apprehension and generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the superknowledges?
The Blessed One replied:

Furthermore, Subhūti, there is no distinction whatsoever between non-apprehension and generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the superknowledges. Moreover, Subhūti, that which is untainted— generosity, ethical discipline,
patience, vigor, meditative absorption, wisdom, and the superknowledges— is likewise non-apprehension.
The distinction between them has been explained.
He asked: "But, Blessed One, how is the distinction between unadulterated generosity and so forth, up to the superknowledges, explained?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift without apprehending the gift, without apprehending the relinquishment, without apprehending the giver, and without apprehending the recipient; he guards his morality without apprehending morality; he practices patience without apprehending patience; and he practices vigor without apprehending vigor.
Not apprehending concentration, he courses in concentration; not apprehending wisdom, he courses in wisdom;

not apprehending the superknowledges, he courses in the superknowledges; not apprehending the foundations of mindfulness, he courses in the foundations of mindfulness; and so on, up to: not apprehending the path, he courses in the path; and so on, up to: not apprehending emptiness, he courses in emptiness. Not apprehending...

He courses in the signless while [perceiving] the signless. Without apprehending anything, he courses in the wishless while [perceiving] the wishless. Without apprehending sentient beings, he brings sentient beings to maturity. Without apprehending a buddha-field, he purifies a buddha-field. Without apprehending the qualities of a Buddha, he awakens to enlightenment. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva—

He courses in the perfection of wisdom that is non-apprehension. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, becomes invincible to Māra the Evil One or to the deities belonging to Māra’s host.
(AdSPG II 11) VII. Abhisamaya (VII a) When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, encompass the six perfections with a single mind? [How does he encompass] the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, and the five powers?"

The seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the three gateways to liberation, the four noble truths, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the five superknowledges, internal emptiness, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature,
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, and great compassion.
"How does he grasp the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), the thirty-two marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*)?
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, whatever gift a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives, it is not otherwise than being embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Whatever ethical discipline he maintains, it is not otherwise than being embraced by the perfection of wisdom."
He is embraced by it.

Whatever patience he cultivates, that is not [accomplished] otherwise than through being embraced by the perfection of wisdom. Whatever vigor he exerts, that is not [accomplished] otherwise than through being embraced by the perfection of wisdom. Whatever meditative concentration he enters, that is not [accomplished] otherwise than through the perfection of wisdom.
He is embraced by it. Whatever wisdom he cultivates, that is not embraced by anything other than the perfection of wisdom.

Whatever meditative absorptions (dhyānas) he enters, that is not embraced by anything other than the perfection of wisdom. Whatever immeasurables (apramāṇas) he enters, that is not embraced by anything other than the perfection of wisdom. This extends to whatever formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) he enters.

It is not otherwise than through being embraced by the perfection of wisdom. When he enters the applications of mindfulness, that is not otherwise than through being embraced by the perfection of wisdom. Up to: when he cultivates the noble eightfold path, that is not otherwise than through being embraced by the perfection of wisdom. When he cultivates the gateways to liberation, that is not otherwise than through the perfection of wisdom.
It is embraced by it. That he cultivates the four noble truths is not otherwise than being embraced by the perfection of wisdom.
That he cultivates the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments is not otherwise than being embraced by the perfection of wisdom. That which... (AdSPG II 12)

When he cultivates the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), that is not possible except through being embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). When he cultivates everything from internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*), that is not possible except through being embraced by the perfection of wisdom.
When he cultivates the ten powers of a Tathāgata (*daśatathāgatabala*), that is not possible except through being embraced by the perfection of wisdom. Up to...

That he cultivates the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is nothing other than being sustained by the perfection of wisdom. That he brings forth the primary marks and the eighty secondary characteristics is nothing other than being sustained by the perfection of wisdom. For it is thus, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, by means of a single production of thought—
He embraces the six perfections; he embraces [them] up to the eighty secondary marks.
He asks: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, embraced by the perfection of wisdom, embrace the six perfections with a single production of thought, up to the eighty secondary marks?
The Blessed One said:

In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift, being embraced by that perfection of wisdom, he does not form a dualistic perception regarding it. When he guards his ethical discipline, he does not form a dualistic perception regarding it. When he cultivates patience, he does not form a dualistic perception regarding it. When he exerts diligence...
In that regard, one does not have the perception of duality. When one cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*), therein one does not have the perception of duality.
When one cultivates wisdom (*prajñā*), therein one does not have the perception of duality. This extends to when one brings forth the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*);
therein, one does not have the perception of duality.

He asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, give a gift and yet not form a dualistic perception therein? And how does he bring forth the eighty secondary marks, and yet not form a dualistic perception therein?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom fulfills the perfection of giving.
Within that perfection of giving, he includes all six perfections and then bestows gifts. In this same way, [he includes] all the factors conducive to awakening..."
He fulfills the dharmas until, having included all six perfections within that path, he cultivates the path. How, then, is that so?
At the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift, he [gives] it in the untainted state.
Abiding in the mind, he gives a gift. Abiding there in that untainted mind, he does not perceive any sign:
"Who gives? or "To whom does one give? or "By what means does one give? or "Who am I who gives? With a mind free from signs—untainted, devoid of craving, and devoid of ignorance—he gives the gift.
He does not perceive that mind; he does not perceive that gift. This should be applied to all the qualities of a Buddha.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom guards his ethical discipline with a mind free from signs; yet he does not perceive that ethical discipline. This should be applied to all the qualities of a Buddha.

Thus, with a mind free from signs, one cultivates patience, yet one does not perceive that patience. This should be applied to all the qualities of a Buddha. With a mind free from signs, one exerts vigor, yet one does not perceive that vigor.

To the extent that it is to be done regarding all the qualities of a Buddha, he enters into meditative concentration with a mind free from signs, yet he does not perceive that concentration. To the extent that it is to be done regarding all the qualities of a Buddha, he cultivates wisdom with a mind free from signs, yet he does not perceive that wisdom. To the extent that it is to be done regarding all the qualities of a Buddha...

It should be practiced. With a mind free from signs (*animitta*), one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and so on up to the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*); this is how it should be practiced.

He asked: "Blessed One, how is there the fulfillment of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) when all phenomena are signless and without conditioned activity? How is there the fulfillment of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom?"
There is the fulfillment of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the noble eightfold path. There is the fulfillment of the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

"How does the fulfillment of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha come about?
The Blessed One said:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift with a mind free from signs (*animitta*): food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink, vehicles to those seeking vehicles, and so on, up to various other human requisites;
or his own internal limbs and members, or external things such as wife, sons, daughters, or kingdom, having adorned them all.
He gives to those who ask.
Suppose someone were to come to him and say, "What is the use of giving such a gift that is so unhelpful?
To that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, it occurs as follows:
Even though sentient beings may revile me, saying, "By giving such an unstable gift as this," nevertheless,
I must indeed give gifts;
it is not that I should not give gifts.
It should be given. Having made that gift common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
He dedicates it in such a way that, while dedicating it, he does not perceive any sign—whether it be "I am giving" or "to whom I am giving."
By what means do I give? Who gives? What do I dedicate? Where do I dedicate? By what means do I dedicate? Who dedicates?
He does not perceive that entity which he might give, nor that place to which he might give it for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One should dedicate it. For what reason?

Because every thing is empty by way of internal emptiness, empty by way of external emptiness, empty by way of internal and external emptiness, empty by way of the emptiness of emptiness, empty by way of great emptiness, empty by way of the emptiness of the conditioned, and empty by way of the emptiness of the unconditioned.

It is empty by way of absolute emptiness; it is empty by way of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end; it is empty by way of the emptiness of dispersion; it is empty by way of the emptiness of intrinsic nature; it is empty by way of the emptiness of all phenomena; it is empty by way of the emptiness of specific characteristics. He perceives thus: "Where will he dedicate? What will he dedicate? By what means will he dedicate?"

By dedicating in this way, he has truly dedicated; he brings sentient beings to maturity, takes hold of a buddha-field, and fulfills the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor,
the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and emptiness.
He fulfills the signless and wishless concentrations, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
From the very beginning, he fulfills the perfection of generosity, yet he does not grasp at its karmic maturation.
It is just as, for example, among the gods who wield power over the creations of others, all perfections of requisites appear by the mere power of their thought.
In this very way, all perfections of requisites appear for that bodhisattva mahāsattva by his mere thought.

By means of that giving, he attends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; he satisfies the world of gods, humans, and asuras. Having embraced those beings through that perfection of giving and with skillful means, he [establishes them] in the three...

He establishes them in the vehicles. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom fulfills the perfection of giving with a mind free from signs. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline, and so on up to the perfection of [giving]?
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline.

He attains the noble, untainted ethical discipline that is included within the path and acquired through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, his ethical discipline is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, unblemished, liberating, well-composed, and praised by the wise.
And by means of that morality, he does not grasp at any phenomenon: whether it be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;

nor the thirty-two marks of a great man; nor the great kṣatriya clans, the great brāhmaṇa clans, or the great householder clans; nor the gods of the Four Great Kings, or those belonging to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
or the Yāma gods, or the Tuṣita gods, or the Nirmāṇarati gods, or the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods;

or the Brahmakāyika gods, or the Brahmapurohita gods, or the Brahmapāriṣadya gods; or the Parītta gods, or the Apramāṇa gods, or the Ābhāsvara gods; or the Pariśubha gods, or the Apramāṇaśubha gods, or the Śubhakṛtsna gods, or the Bṛhatphala gods, or the Asaṃjñika gods, or the Aspr̥ha gods, or the Atapa gods.

or the Sudṛśa or Sudarśana or Aghaniṣṭha [heavens], or the sphere of infinite space, or the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; or the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship; or a pratyekabuddha, or the sovereign dominion of a universal monarch—thinking, "May I cause these to come to pass."

Except that, having made them common to all sentient beings together, he dedicates them toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) by means of a dedication that is signless (*animitta*), non-apprehensible (*anupalambha*), and non-dual;

this is according to worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) and not, however, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). And by means of that perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) being fulfilled through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), [he attains it].
And he produces the four meditative absorptions (dhyāna) by way of non-attachment. He also brings forth the divine eye (divya-cakṣus).

With that divine eye, which is capable of conversion, he sees those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the eastern direction, teaching the Dharma; and his vision of them does not fail, as long as—

He has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Likewise, he sees the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who dwell, abide, and maintain themselves, and who teach the Dharma, in the southern direction, the western, the northern, and indeed throughout all the ten directions; and that vision of theirs does not perish until he reaches unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Having attained perfect enlightenment, with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears the speech of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they speak. And that which has been heard does not perish until the welfare of both himself and others has been accomplished by means of that hearing. And by means of the knowledge of the movements of the minds of those Buddhas...
He understands the minds of the Blessed Ones with his own mind. And by means of that knowledge of the movements of the minds of others, he acts for the benefit of all sentient beings;

and by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, having discerned the past roots of virtue of those beings, he demonstrates, encourages, inspires, and gladdens them by means of those roots of virtue.
Once they have been thus exhorted and thus gladdened, they proceed toward excellence;

and by means of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), he establishes beings in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*) up to establishing them in arhatship. He establishes them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment;
he establishes them in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*). In this way, wherever beings are capable, [he establishes them].
He establishes them in wholesome qualities here and there. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline with a mind free from signs.
And how, Subhūti, does he fulfill the perfection of patience regarding phenomena that are signless, effortless, unapprehendable, and unconditioned?

In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening until the time he sits upon the seat of awakening, even if all sentient beings were to come repeatedly and strike him with clods of earth, sticks, or weapons, the bodhisattva mahāsattva must not allow even a single moment of mental agitation accompanied by resentment to arise. In that situation, the bodhisattva...

A mahāsattva should cultivate two kinds of patience. Which two? First, that which consists in my enduring all beings—namely, their reviling, abuse, and blows with clods of earth, sticks, or weapons. Second, the patience regarding non-arising phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) which is to be produced. In this regard, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
When being reviled or abused, or when being struck with clods of earth, sticks, or weapons, one should reflect in this way:
"Who is reviling me? Who is abusing me? Or who is inflicting these blows with clods, sticks, and weapons? To whom are they being inflicted?
Thereby, one should reflect upon the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

While examining the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, one will not apprehend even phenomena themselves; how much less so a phenomenon that has an intrinsic nature? As he thus examines the intrinsic nature of phenomena, it occurs to him: "Who cuts me, or who pierces me?
Examining the intrinsic nature of phenomena in this way, he will attain the patient acceptance of non-arising phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
In that regard, what is the patient acceptance of non-arising phenomena?

It is the non-arising of afflictions and the indestructibility of gnosis. Abiding in these two forms of patient acceptance, he will fulfill the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
...up to the noble eightfold path, the three gateways to liberation, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges,
great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Abiding in these dharmas— which are noble, untainted, supramundane, and uncommon to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—

Then, together with that, she will fulfill the noble superknowledges. Through those superknowledges, when they are fulfilled, she fully realizes the six perfections and the five untainted superknowledges.

Abiding there, he will see the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the eastern direction with his divine eye. Having seen those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, he will attain the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). That recollection of the Buddha will not be interrupted for him until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. This applies likewise throughout the ten directions, all around.
With the divine ear-element, he will retain everything spoken by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;

having retained it, he will teach the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of suchness. He will know the minds of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, with his own mind. By means of that knowledge of the movements of the mind, he will know the minds of all sentient beings with his own mind.

He will teach the Dharma for the sake of suchness. By means of the knowledge that recollects past lives, having understood the roots of goodness of those beings, he will gladden them and inspire them with their former roots of goodness; and by means of the knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows, he will establish and settle those beings in the three vehicles. That Bodhisattva, indeed...

The Mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, having matured sentient beings through skill in means and purified the Buddha-field, practices in the knowledge of all aspects, fulfills the knowledge of all aspects, awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will turn the wheel of Dharma. It is in this way, Subhūti, that for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—
For one practicing the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of patience is fulfilled.

And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of vigor regarding phenomena that are signless, effortless, non-apprehendable, non-manifesting, and unconditioned?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is endowed with physical vigor. Having attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna, he dwells having attained each of the dhyānas up to the fourth. Having entered the fourth dhyāna, he experiences various kinds of miraculous powers.

He touches the sun and moon with his hand and exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world. Endowed with that physical vigor, he goes by means of his supernormal power to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who dwell in the eastern direction across many hundreds of thousands of myriads of world-systems, and attends upon those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

His requisites— robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for use in sickness— will not be exhausted until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. And once he has awakened to enlightenment,
the world with its gods, humans, and asuras will become happy through those requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for use in sickness.

And when [the Buddha] has entered final nirvana, worship of the relics proceeds within his remains. By that very same exercise of supernatural power (*ṛddhy-abhisaṃskāra*), he goes and hears the Dharma from those Blessed Buddhas in their presence. And as it was heard, it never perishes, until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and brings sentient beings to maturity.

And while practicing for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he takes hold of a buddha-field. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with physical vigor fulfills the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).
And how, Subhūti, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with mental vigor that is noble?
How does one fulfill the perfection of vigor by means of the untainted path included within the path?

Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, endowed with mental vigor, allows no opportunity for unwholesome bodily action and allows no opportunity for unwholesome vocal action.

He does not grasp at it as either permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as conditioned or unconditioned; nor as the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; nor as the realm with outflows or the realm without outflows; nor as the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.

Or loving-kindness, or compassion, or sympathetic joy, or equanimity; or the sphere of infinite space, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; or the foundations of mindfulness, or the right efforts, or the bases of psychic power, or the faculties, or the powers, or the factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path; or emptiness, or the signless, or the wishless; up to the qualities of a Buddha.

Or he does not grasp at them as being permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self; nor does he grasp at the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, solitary enlightenment, or the state of a bodhisattva. These beings are manifested through vision.
"These are characterized by the stage of the attenuated [defilements], these are characterized by the lower fetters, these are characterized by the higher fetters;

these are characterized by the Pratyekabuddhas, these are characterized by the knowledge of the aspects of the path, these are characterized by the knowledge of all aspects"—even in this way, he does not grasp at them. For what reason?

For indeed, their intrinsic nature does not exist, by which intrinsic nature they might be manifested. Endowed with that very same mental vigor, even when facing the jaws of death, he acts for the benefit of sentient beings;
yet he does not apprehend those sentient beings. He fulfills the perfection of vigor, yet he does not apprehend that perfection of vigor, nor the qualities of a Buddha.

He fulfills those qualities of a Buddha, yet he does not apprehend them. He purifies a buddha-field, yet he does not apprehend that buddha-field. Endowed with that physical and mental vigor, he fulfills all wholesome dharmas, yet he is not attached to them. Being unattached, he [does not cling] to a buddha-field.

He travels to Buddha-fields, performing the welfare of sentient beings, manifesting transformations through whatever supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) he desires. He manifests by means of that supernatural power:
whether by a rain of flowers, or by the emission of fragrances, or by the performance of song and instrumental music, or by an earthquake, or by a radiance of light.

Or by manifesting a world-system composed of the seven precious jewels; or wherever he relinquishes himself for the sake of beings who desire youth; or if he relinquishes himself for the sake of beings blind from birth;
or if he emits fragrances; or if he performs great sacrifices where no taking of life occurs.
Or else, he leads infinite sentient beings onto the path; he restrains them from taking life, and so on, up to liberating them from wrong views.
He favors some with generosity, others with ethical discipline. For the sake of some, he relinquishes his limbs and members;
for some, his children and wife; for some, his kingdom; and for the sake of others, he offers up his very self. Thus, by whatever means possible—

He must accomplish the welfare of sentient beings by whatever means necessary; thus he accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, endowed with mental vigor regarding signless phenomena, fulfills the perfection of vigor.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, abide in phenomena that are nameless and signless and fulfill the perfection of concentration?

Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom fulfills all other concentrations except for the concentration of a Tathāgata. He remains detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states.

Free from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with rapture and pleasure. With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and so on, up to a mind imbued with equanimity, he pervades the entire world and, having attained it, dwells therein. This continues up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Having attained it, he dwells therein. Abiding in that perfection of concentration (*samādhipāramitā*), he enters into and emerges from the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) in forward and reverse order. He attains and dwells in the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvasamāpatti*), the emptiness concentration (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the signless concentration (*ānimitta-samādhi*), and the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*). And he attains the uninterrupted concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*).
He dwells; having attained the lightning-like concentration and the diamond-like concentration, which is right concentration, he dwells.

Abiding here in this perfection of concentration, he dwells having fully attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Abiding here in this perfection of concentration, by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path, [he proceeds] as far as the knowledge of the aspects of the path.

Having seen that all meditative concentrations are included therein, he transcends the stage of pure insight (*śuklavipaśyanābhūmi*), and having transcended the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the eighth stage, the stage of vision (*darśanabhūmi*),

the stage of refinement (*tanubhūmi*), the stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāgabhūmi*), the stage of one who has completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvibhūmi*), and the stage of the solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddhabhūmi*), he enters the bodhisattva’s determination (*nyāma*). He fulfills the stage of a buddha and courses within these stages.
And yet, he does not attain the fruit in the interim, as long as he has not attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*).

Abiding here in this perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhipāramitā*), he travels from buddha-field to buddha-field, attending upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. He attends upon those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and [hears] from those Buddhas...

He plants roots of merit in the presence of the Blessed Ones. He brings sentient beings to maturity. He purifies a buddha-field. He travels from world-system to world-system. He acts for the benefit of sentient beings;
he favors some sentient beings with generosity, and others with ethical discipline.
By means of patience for some, vigor for others, meditative concentration for others, wisdom for others, liberation for others, and the knowledge and vision of liberation for others,

he establishes some beings in the fruit of stream-entry; he establishes some in the fruit of once-returning, some in the fruit of non-returning, some in arhatship, and some in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.

He establishes some in awakening. He engages those beings in whatever roots of goodness and dharmas by which they may emerge. Abiding here in this perfection of meditative concentration, he brings forth all the gateways of dhāraṇīs, attains the four analytical knowledges, and becomes a possessor of the superknowledges that result from maturation.

He is never again born in a mother’s womb; he never indulges in sensual pleasures, nor is there any birth that he does not assume. Yet, he is never defiled by the faults of those births. Why is that? Because he has clearly seen all phenomena as being like an illusion. Having understood all conditioned things to be like an illusion, he...
He acts for the benefit of all sentient beings, yet therein neither sentient beings nor the designation "sentient being" is apprehended.

Not apprehending any phenomena, he establishes sentient beings in non-apprehension alone, by recourse to worldly convention and not, however, from the perspective of ultimate truth. Abiding here in this perfection of concentration, [he abides] in all meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.

He practices and is never deprived of the perfection of meditative concentration until he fulfills unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Abiding here in the knowledge of the aspects of the path, he brings forth the knowledge of all aspects. Abiding therein, he abandons all traces of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-anusandhi*). Having abandoned all traces of habitual tendencies, for both himself and others...

And he accomplishes the welfare of others. By accomplishing the welfare of both himself and others, he becomes one worthy of offerings for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom fulfills the perfection of concentration.

(VII 2) And how, Subhūti, does the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reach fulfillment for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom regarding signless phenomena? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any phenomenon as truly existent or as fully established; he does not perceive the true existence or the full establishment of form. Nor does he perceive the true existence or the full establishment of feeling, perception, or mental formations.
He does not perceive the existence or the perfected nature of consciousness. He does not perceive the arising of form;

he does not perceive the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Not perceiving the arising of form, and not perceiving the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, he [sees] this gateway to form.
He does not perceive [them]. He does not perceive an entrance-gate for the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not perceive an accumulation of form; he does not perceive an accumulation of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. (AdSPG II 22)
In this way, up to the point that he does not perceive an entrance for the arising of either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena;
he perceives them only as empty and hollow. Examining in this manner, he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form (*rūpa*);
he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*). Up to...
He does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of phenomena, whether they are with outflows or without outflows.
Practicing in the perfection of wisdom, he resolves that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.
Resolving thus, while practicing in internal emptiness, up to and including the practice in the emptiness of specific characteristics, he does not...
He does not become attached to any phenomena—whether to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including awakening.
Practicing the perfection of wisdom, which has non-existence as its intrinsic nature, he fulfills the path of a bodhisattva;
that is to say, the six perfections, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the four [fearlessnesses].

He fulfills the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the eighty minor marks;

he stands upon the path to enlightenment characterized by maturation, until the six perfections are fulfilled, up to the fulfillment of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and finally the superknowledges that result from maturation.

Those beings who are to be assisted by means of generosity, he assists them with generosity; those who are to be assisted by means of ethical discipline, he assists them with ethical discipline; those who are to be assisted by means of patience, he assists them with patience; those who are to be assisted by means of vigor, he assists them with vigor; those who are to be assisted by means of meditative concentration, he assists them with meditative concentration.

He takes hold of them. Those who are to be assisted by wisdom, he assists with wisdom; those who are to be assisted by liberation, he assists with liberation; those who are to be assisted by the knowledge and vision of liberation, he assists with the knowledge and vision of liberation; and those who are to be established in the fruit of stream-entry, he establishes them in the fruit of stream-entry.

Those who are to be established in the fruit of once-returning, he establishes them in the fruit of once-returning; those who are to be established in the fruit of non-returning, he establishes them in the fruit of non-returning; those who are to be established in arhatship, he establishes them in arhatship; those who are to be established in individual enlightenment, he establishes them in individual enlightenment.

He establishes them. Those who are to be established in awakening, he establishes in awakening. This is the abbreviated formula for all cases. Manifesting various kinds of miraculous transformations, he goes to world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; and if he so desires, those world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—
Whatever kind of jewels he may desire for those world-systems, he will manifest such jewels. Fulfilling the intentions of sentient beings, he will go from one world-system to another;

having seen those world-systems, he will take possession of a Buddha-field according to his wish. Just as there are enjoyments and pleasures among the gods of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), even those things which exist in other Buddha-fields where seeking has ceased will be present there for him. By means of that ripening...

By means of the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom;

by means of the superknowledges resulting from maturation and the path to awakening resulting from maturation—while practicing in the knowledge of the aspects of the path—he will attain the fulfillment of all phenomena and reach the knowledge of all aspects. This applies as far as form is ungrasped, and feeling, perception, and mental formations [are likewise ungrasped].

Consciousness is unappropriated, as are all phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome, mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—they are all unappropriated.
In the very same way, for one who has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, all enjoyments and usages in that buddha-field will be unappropriated. Why is that?

For all phenomena are ungraspable through the yoga of non-apprehension; indeed, the Dharma has been taught for the sake of the non-grasping of all beings. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the perfection of wisdom through the yoga of the signless.
Chapter 72. Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"How, O Blessed One, [is it] regarding all dharmas that are undifferentiated, all dharmas that are signless, and all dharmas that are empty of their own characteristics?"

There is the fulfillment of the cultivation of the six perfections: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom. How is the distinction between these phenomena—both those with outflows and those without outflows—perceived?
How is it that the perfection of generosity is included within the perfection of wisdom?

How are the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration included? And how is it that everything up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is included within the perfection of wisdom? Blessed One, how is this so for those things which are thus of such different characteristics?
"How does there come to be a designation for phenomena that have a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, [he perceives] the five [aggregates] as being like a dream."
Abiding in the five aggregates, one gives gifts, guards morality, cultivates patience, exerts vigor, cultivates concentration, and cultivates wisdom—
abiding in the five aggregates which are like an echo, one gives gifts, guards morality, and cultivates patience.

He exerts vigor, cultivates concentration, and cultivates wisdom. Thus, abiding in the five aggregates—which are like a reflection, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a magical creation—he gives gifts, guards his ethical discipline, cultivates patience, exerts vigor, cultivates concentration, and cultivates wisdom. The five aggregates are like a dream.
The five aggregates are without characteristics; they are like an echo, like a reflection, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a magical creation. Why is that?
Because a dream has no intrinsic nature, a reflection has no intrinsic nature, and a mirage has no intrinsic nature.
There is no intrinsic nature in an illusion, there is no intrinsic nature in a magical creation, and there is no intrinsic nature in anything else.
That which has no intrinsic nature has no characteristic;
that which has no characteristic is of one single characteristic, namely, the absence of characteristics. Therefore, Subhūti, by this method you should understand it thus:

Giving is without marks; the giver is without marks; the recipient is without marks. He who, knowing this, gives a gift, fulfills the perfection of giving and does not turn back from the perfection of ethical discipline. He does not turn back from the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom. He remains here within these six perfections.

Abiding therein, he fulfills the four dhyānas. He fulfills the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments. He fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. [He fulfills] internal emptiness...

He fulfills external emptiness and internal-external emptiness; he fulfills the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, up to the emptiness of specific characteristics. He fulfills the concentration of emptiness;
he fulfills the signless concentration and the wishless concentration. He fulfills the eight liberations.
He fulfills the nine successive attainments. He fulfills the five superknowledges. He fulfills hundreds of doors of the five dhāraṇīs.
He fulfills the four analytical knowledges.
[He fulfills] the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

He fulfills the qualities of a Buddha. Abiding here in these ripened, untainted dharmas, he travels by means of supernatural power to the world-systems in the eastern direction and attends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. He serves them and benefits sentient beings with all manner of enjoyments and necessities; those who are to be gathered through giving, he gathers through giving.

He gathers them in. Those who are to be gathered by means of ethical discipline, he gathers by means of ethical discipline; those who are to be gathered by means of patience, he gathers by means of patience; those who are to be gathered by means of vigor, he gathers by means of vigor; those who are to be gathered by means of meditative concentration, he gathers by means of meditative concentration; those who are to be gathered by means of wisdom, he gathers by means of wisdom.

He gathers [beings]. To the extent that those who are to be gathered by all wholesome dharmas are to be gathered, he gathers them with all wholesome dharmas. Endowed with those roots of goodness, he becomes a sovereign over all dharmas and yet takes up cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
However, he is not defiled by the sufferings belonging to cyclic existence. For the sake of sentient beings, he takes up the prosperity of gods and humans.
By means of those excellences with which he gathers in sentient beings, he knows all phenomena to be without marks. He knows the fruit of stream-entry, yet he does not abide therein.
He knows the fruit of once-returning, yet he does not abide therein. He knows the fruit of non-returning, yet he does not...
He abides therein; yet he knows arhatship and does not abide therein. He knows the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and does not abide therein. Why is that?
Because, having known all phenomena, he must attain the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).

These are the qualities not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having realized that all dharmas are without marks (alakṣaṇa), knows the six perfections to be without marks; indeed, he knows all the buddha-dharmas to be without marks.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, [he perceives] things comparable to a dream...

Abiding in the five aggregates of clinging, he fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline. Abiding in the five aggregates of clinging—which are like an echo, like a reflection, like an illusion, like a mirage, and like a magical creation—he fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline. Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva [regards] the five aggregates of clinging as being like a dream.

Having known the five aggregates of clinging to be like an echo, like a reflection, like an illusion, like a mirage, and like a magical creation, and having known them thus, he fulfills the perfection of morality that is without characteristics— morality that is unbroken, untorn, unspotted, unblemished, unpolluted, liberating, praised by the wise, well-perfected, noble, and included within the path that is free from outflows.

The supramundane, abiding in which one maintains the morality of conventional undertaking; and the morality acquired through the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the morality of restraint, the morality of informative expression, the morality of active practice, and the morality of non-active practice. He, being of such a form...
Endowed with moral discipline, he does not grasp at it, thinking: "By means of this, may I be reborn into the company of great kṣatriya families;

or may I be reborn into the company of great brahmin families, or into the company of great householder families; or may I become a universal monarch, or a regional king, or a member of the assembly of the Four Great Kings."

Or may I be reborn into the company of the gods; may I be reborn into the company of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, or the Yāma gods, or the Tuṣita gods, or the Nirmāṇarati gods, or the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods. Or may I attain the fruit of stream-entry, or that of a once-returner, or a non-returner, or arhatship. Or [may I attain] pratyekabodhi.
or might attain awakening. Why is that?

Because all phenomena are without marks; they have a single mark, namely, the mark of having non-existence as their intrinsic nature. For a phenomenon without marks does not attain a phenomenon without marks, nor does a phenomenon with different marks attain a phenomenon with different marks.
Nor do phenomena that are non-distinctive or without characteristics attain phenomena that are non-distinctive or without characteristics.

It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the perfection of morality without characteristics and enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva. Entering the fixed course of a bodhisattva, [he dwells] in the non-arising [dharmas].
He attains patience regarding all phenomena. Practicing in the knowledge of the aspects of the path, he attains the five superknowledges born of maturation;

having established himself in five hundred gateways of dhāraṇīs and five hundred gateways of samādhis, and having attained the four analytical knowledges, he will travel from buddhafield to buddhafield, attending upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

He brings sentient beings to maturity and will take hold of a buddha-field. He will wander through the saṃsāra of the five destinies, yet he will not be defiled by the karma belonging to saṃsāra nor by its maturation. It is just as if, for example, an emanation were to walk, stand, sit, or lie down.
Neither his coming is perceived, nor his going, nor his standing, nor his sitting, nor his lying down;

yet he works for the benefit of sentient beings, and yet no sentient being is apprehended, nor even the designation "sentient being. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, there were a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śānta.

Having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and having turned the wheel of Dharma after awakening to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and having led immeasurable beings to final nirvana by means of two vehicles, he did not perceive any bodhisattva whom he had prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. He [then] [withdrew] his life-formations...
Having cast off that which was created and having manifested another creation, he passes away into the realm of nirvana without remainder of substrate.

Furthermore, Subhūti, after the passing of an eon, that very creation, having bestowed a prophecy upon a bodhisattva mahāsattva regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, passes away into final nirvana. And when he has passed away, there is no entity whatsoever remaining.

is apprehended—whether it be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. In the very same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend a sentient being, nor the designation "sentient being," yet he acts for the benefit of sentient beings. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Through the fulfillment of which...
All phenomena are contained within it.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he abides in the five aggregates of clinging which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like an illusion, and like a mirage.
Abiding in the five aggregates of clinging which are like a magical creation, how does one fulfill the perfection of patience characterized by the absence of marks (*alakṣaṇakṣāntipāramitā*)?
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in dharmas that are without marks, fulfill the perfection of patience?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of patience through two kinds of patience. What are these two kinds of patience?
