Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having seen that all these dharmas are empty, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings who have fallen into perverted views. He teaches it in such a way that he does not abide even in the emptinesses themselves. Seeing all dharmas in this manner and knowing them to be without obstruction, he does not disturb any dharma, nor does he divide it into two.
And he teaches according to reality. It is just as if a Tathāgata, having emanated many millions of emanations,

were to direct some toward the perfection of generosity, some toward the perfection of ethical discipline, some toward the perfection of patience, some toward the perfection of vigor, and some toward the perfection of meditative concentration.

He directs some toward the perfection of wisdom; some toward the four meditative concentrations; some toward the four immeasurables; some toward the four formless attainments; some toward the four applications of mindfulness; he directs some toward as many as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; and he directs some toward as many as the knowledge of all aspects.

He establishes some in the fruit of stream-entry; he establishes others, up to and including, in awakening. What do you think, Subhūti? Has any dharma been differentiated by that emanation? He replied: "Certainly not, Lord."
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Subhūti, by this method you should understand it thus: how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings."
And he establishes them in accordance with reality; he liberates them from the perversions by means of the yoga of being neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, form is neither bound nor liberated;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the non-boundness and non-liberatedness of form is not form. That which is the non-boundness and non-liberatedness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness; and so on, up to: that which is the non-boundness and non-liberatedness of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is not those conditioned and unconditioned phenomena. For what reason?

For form is utterly pure, and so on, up to consciousness which is utterly pure; this applies to all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, yet does not apprehend a "sentient being. This is because all phenomena are non-apprehensible.

The bodhisattva mahāsattva stands by way of non-abiding; that is, by way of non-abiding through the emptiness of form, up to and including by way of non-abiding through the emptiness of consciousness, and even by way of non-abiding through the emptiness of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena. For conditioned and unconditioned phenomena do not abide anywhere. Why is that?
For their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not apprehended, wherein they might be established.

Indeed, a non-entity (abhāva) will not abide in a non-entity; an intrinsic nature will not abide in an intrinsic nature; and an extrinsic nature (parabhāva) will not abide in an extrinsic nature. Why is that? Because all of them are not apprehended. And that which is non-apprehension will not abide anywhere. Thus...
Indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom elucidates these dharmas by means of these all-empty states;
it is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] in the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, one becomes free from offense toward the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, the Pratyekabuddhas, the Śrāvakas, and all Noble Ones.

For it is precisely this very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) that has been realized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas; having realized it, they teach the Dharma to all sentient beings.

They do not deviate from that true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena. Why is that? Because the true nature does not deviate; neither suchness (*tathatā*) nor the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) deviates. Why is that?
Because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist, such that it could deviate.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "If, Blessed One, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) does not deviate, nor does suchness (*tathatā*), nor the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), then, Blessed One, is form one thing and the realm of phenomena another, is suchness another, and the limit of reality another— up to [and including]..."

"Is consciousness one thing, the dharma-realm another, suchness another, and the limit of reality another; even so, are conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, mundane and supramundane phenomena, and tainted and untainted phenomena all one thing, while the dharma-realm is another, suchness is another, and the limit of reality is another?
The Blessed One said:
It is not so, Subhūti;

it is not so, Subhūti, that form is one thing and the dharma-realm another, that suchness is another, or that the limit of reality is another; nor, up to and including, is consciousness one thing and the dharma-realm another, that suchness is another, or that the limit of reality is another; indeed, all dharmas are not different [from them].
"The realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is one thing, suchness (*tathatā*) is another, and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is yet another.
He said: "If, Blessed One, form is not one thing and the realm of phenomena another, suchness another, and the limit of reality another;
and if, up to and including, consciousness is not one thing and the realm of phenomena another, suchness another, and the limit of reality another..."

If all phenomena are one thing, the realm of phenomena another, suchness another, and the limit of reality another, then, Blessed One, how does this distinction come to be? That is, how is there a dark ripening for dark phenomena,
whether it be rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama?
The ripening of white dharmas is white:
gods and humans;
the ripening of black-and-white dharmas is black-and-white.
The experience of pleasure and pain. The maturation of non-black and non-white dharmas is non-black and non-white:
the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, up to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, it is by taking conventional truth as the standard that the establishment of the fruits is taught;
however, the establishment of the fruits cannot be taught by means of ultimate truth. Why is that?
Because that dharma is non-conceptual and inexpressible.

That is to say: the truth of name, the truth of form, non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification—this is extreme emptiness, the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end.
He said: "Blessed One, if the establishment of the fruits [of the path] occurs by relying upon conventional truth, and not by ultimate truth..."

"But, Blessed One, will all foolish commoners attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, and perfect complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One said:
Furthermore, Subhūti, do foolish ordinary persons understand conventional truth or ultimate truth?

If they did understand them, then for them too there would be an establishment of fruits—whether the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even perfect complete enlightenment. But as for those who...
Subhūti, for foolish common people there is no path, no establishment of the path, and no cultivation of the path;
how then could there be an establishment of the fruits for foolish common people?
For noble persons, however, there is both the path and the cultivation of the path; therefore, there will be an establishment of the fruits for noble persons.
He asked: "But, Blessed One, does the attainment of the fruit result from the cultivation of the path? Or is the fruit attained?
The Blessed One said: "Not so, Subhūti."

There is no attainment of the fruit through the cultivation of the path, nor is a fruit attained [in that way]. Yet, Subhūti, it is not the case that one who has not cultivated the path attains the fruit, nor is the fruit attained by means of a path. For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom establishes the fruits for sentient beings, yet without partitioning the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*).
Or is the establishment of the fruit [based] on the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm?

He said: "Blessed One, if the establishment of the fruit does not occur through a division of portions of either the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm, then why has it been taught by the Blessed One?"
This is the fruit of stream-entry through the abandonment of the three fetters;
the fruit of once-returning through the attenuation of sensual desire and ill will;
and the fruit of non-returning through the abandonment of the five lower fetters.
Arhatship is the abandonment of the five higher fetters;

Pratyekabuddhahood is the realization that whatever has the nature of arising all has the nature of cessation; and Perfect Enlightenment is the abandonment of all latencies and their continuations. O Blessed One, regarding this speech of yours—
"How should we understand this meaning:
that the establishment of the fruits [of the path] does not occur through a partitioning of conditioned or unconditioned phenomena?
The Blessed One said:

"Furthermore, Subhūti, is the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship, or pratyekabuddhahood, or unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—these conditioned or are they unconditioned? He replied: "These are unconditioned, Blessed One; they are not conditioned, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:
"But, Subhūti, is there any division of parts in an unconditioned dharma?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? At the time when a son of good family or a daughter of good family penetrates conditioned and unconditioned phenomena as having a single characteristic—that is to say, as being without characteristics—at that time, does there exist anything [for them]?"
"He makes a division of the Dharma: 'It is conditioned' or 'it is unconditioned'?
He said: 'Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:"

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom teaches the Dharma to sentient beings by means of non-interruption; that is to say, by means of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of specific characteristics. He himself does not adhere to any phenomenon whatsoever, nor does he cause another to adhere to anything at all.

Whether in the perfection of generosity, or the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of patience, or the perfection of vigor, or the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom;
or in the first dhyāna, up to the fourth dhyāna; or in loving-kindness, or compassion, or sympathetic joy.

Whether it be in equanimity, or up to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or in the applications of mindfulness, up to the noble eightfold path, or even in omniscience— he, being unattached, does not cling anywhere. It is just as if, for example, an emanation of a Tathāgata were to give a gift.
And he does not cling to the fruit of giving; he does not experience the fruit of giving except for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa.

Likewise, with respect to the six perfections, and even with respect to all phenomena—whether with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned—he does not abide anywhere. It is just so, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
He courses in all phenomena; he does not abide in any phenomenon, nor does he cling to them. Why is that?
Because he has thoroughly penetrated the true nature of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa).
This concludes the seventy-third chapter: The Perfection of the Exposition on the Production of the Primary Marks, the Secondary Characteristics, and the Syllables.
(AdSPG II 60) Chapter 74.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, how is the characteristic of phenomena thoroughly penetrated?
The Blessed One replied:
“Subhūti, it is just as there is no active engagement in desire, hatred, or delusion by a magically created being; there is no active engagement with forms.”

...up to consciousness. Thus, there is non-occurrence with respect to internal and external phenomena; non-occurrence with respect to latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and outbursts (*paryutthāna*); non-occurrence with respect to contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena; non-occurrence with respect to mundane and supramundane, conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; non-occurrence on the path; and non-occurrence in the fruit. Such, Subhūti, is the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ dharmanaya*).
It is well-penetrated.
He asked: "Blessed One, how does the cultivation of the path occur for a magical creation?
The Blessed One said:
Relying upon that cultivation of the path, one is neither defiled nor purified, and is not seen at all within the saṃsāra of the five destinies.
He asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva penetrate all phenomena as being without substance?"
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Does there exist any entity whatsoever belonging to a Tathāgata’s emanation, by depending upon which entity it might become afflicted or purified?"
"Or would it be seen within the saṃsāra of the five destinies?

He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. Blessed One, there is no entity whatsoever belonging to a Tathāgata’s emanation by means of which it could become defiled or purified, or by which it could be seen within the saṃsāra of the five destinies."

The Blessed One said: "It is indeed thus, Subhūti, that the systematic principle of dharmas is thoroughly penetrated. Subhūti asked: "But, Blessed One, is all form like a magical creation of a Tathāgata? Are all feeling, perception, mental formations, and all consciousness like a magical creation of a Tathāgata?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, all form is like a magical creation; all feeling, perception, mental formations, and all consciousness are like magical creations.
Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does the personal effort of a bodhisattva mahāsattva come about?"
If all form is like a magical creation, and so on, up to all consciousness being like a magical creation, then, Blessed One, for that which is a magical creation there is no form,

no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness. There is neither affliction nor purification, nor even a fivefold cyclic existence from which sentient beings might be liberated.
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? While practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive any sentient being whom he might liberate from hell, or from the animal realm, or from the world of Yama, or from among gods or humans?"
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. No sentient being whatsoever has been apprehended by a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
He would liberate [beings] from the triple world. For by him all phenomena have been known, seen, and understood as being like an illusion;
they have been known, seen, and understood as being like a magical creation.
He said: "If, Blessed One, all phenomena have been known by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva as being like an illusion and like a magical creation..."
It has been seen and known. For what purpose, then, does the bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the six perfections?

He practices the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five superknowledges, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the path to awakening; and he purifies the buddha-field.
"And how does he bring sentient beings to maturity?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, if sentient beings themselves knew all phenomena to be like magical emanations, [they would not need to be brought to maturity]."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva would not practice the conduct of a bodhisattva for incalculable eons for the sake of sentient beings were it not for this reason, Subhūti: because sentient beings themselves do not know that all phenomena are like magical illusions, therefore the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections for incalculable eons; he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the buddha-field.
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, all dharmas are like a dream, like an echo, like a mirage, like a reflection, like an illusion,
and like a magical creation, then, Blessed One, where do sentient beings abide, from which a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should lead them away]?"
“While practicing the perfection of wisdom, does one cause them to rise up?
The Blessed One said:

“Subhūti, beings are established in names and signs; they are based on unreal conceptualization. Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he causes them to rise up from those names and signs.”
He asked: "Blessed One, what is name and what is sign?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, this name is adventitious and superimposed, namely, "name" or "sign.
This name is artificial, namely, "name" or "sign"; or "form," or "feeling," or "perception," or "volitional formations," or "consciousness"; or "woman," or "man," or "boy," or "girl."
Or as hell-beings, or as animals, or as beings of the world of Yama; or as gods, or as humans;

or as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), or as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*); or as the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), or as the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), or as the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), or as arhatship, or as the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabodhi*), or as perfect complete enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Or rather, Subhūti, all these designated phenomena are merely names according to their referents. All this conditioned world is name-only, wherein foolish ordinary people are attached;
the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom and endowed with skillful means, discerns this: "All this is a name arisen from conceptual construction."
Do not cling to conceptual constructions. Since things do not exist and are empty of intrinsic nature, wise ones do not adhere to phenomena that are empty.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings through skillful means. What, Subhūti, is a sign?
Subhūti, there are these two signs to which foolish ordinary people are attached. What are the two? Namely, the sign of form and the sign of the formless. And what, Subhūti, is the sign of form?
Whatever form there is, Subhūti—whether gross or subtle, inferior or superior—which exists among these momentary [phenomena]...
Through conceptual construction, one grasps at phenomena; this is called the sign of form (*rūpanimitta*). And what, Subhūti, is the sign of the formless (*ārūpyanimitta*)?

Whatever affliction arises from grasping at the signs of any formless phenomena through conceptual construction—this is called the sign of the formless. A bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, having separated [beings] from that sign by means of skillful means, establishes them in the signless realm (*ānimittadhātu*).

He establishes them in such a way and settles them in such a way that they do not fall into duality— namely, "this is a sign" and "this is signless. Subhūti, it is in this manner that a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
practicing in the perfection of wisdom through skill in means, detaches beings from signs and establishes them in the signless realm.

He said: "If, Blessed One, all these phenomena are ultimately such that they have names and signs as their limit, being mere designations arisen from conceptual construction, then how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, personally attain distinction among wholesome qualities? And how does he establish others in the attainment of distinction among wholesome qualities?"
Regarding phenomena: by means of those wholesome phenomena, one fulfills stage after stage and establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles.
The Blessed One said:
"If, Subhūti, there were a real entity and not a non-entity, it would be a sign. This, Subhūti, is not [taught] in the perfection of wisdom."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing, were to attain distinction regarding wholesome dharmas, he would not establish others in the attainment of distinction. However, Subhūti, because a sign is a non-entity and not a real entity,
therefore a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom fulfills the perfection of meditation.

By means of the yoga of the signless, he fulfills the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity through the yoga of the signless. He fulfills the four meditative concentrations through the yoga of the signless. He fulfills the four immeasurables through the yoga of the signless. He fulfills the four formless attainments through the yoga of the signless.

He fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness by means of the yoga of the signless. He fulfills the noble eightfold path by means of the yoga of the signless. He fulfills internal emptiness by means of the yoga of the signless. He fulfills external emptiness by means of the yoga of the signless. He fulfills internal and external emptiness by means of the yoga of the signless, up to and including the emptiness of specific characteristics.

He fulfills them through the yoga of the signless. He fulfills the eight liberations through the yoga of the signless. He fulfills the nine successive attainments through the yoga of the signless. He fulfills the ten powers of a Tathāgata through the yoga of the signless, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, fulfilling them through the yoga of the signless. He [cultivates] these wholesome dharmas...

Having fulfilled [these], he establishes others in these very same wholesome dharmas by means of the yoga of the signless (*animitta*). Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were even a single sign (*nimitta*) among dharmas, even as small as the tip of a hair, then, Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva would not be [practicing] in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Practicing the signless, the non-recollection, and the non-mental engagement, he will fully awaken to the Dharma. And he will establish sentient beings in suchness within the outflow-free dharmas;

for indeed, Subhūti, all outflow-free dharmas are signless, non-recollection, and non-mental engagement. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings by means of outflow-free dharmas.

He said: "If, Blessed One, all phenomena are signless, without recollection, and without mental engagement, then from where, Blessed One, shall I make this enumeration: 'these are contaminated phenomena, these are uncontaminated phenomena, these are common phenomena, these are uncommon phenomena, these are the phenomena of śrāvakas, these are the phenomena of pratyekabuddhas, and these are the phenomena of bodhisattvas'?"
"Are these the qualities of a Buddha?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti, is the signless one thing and the qualities of a śrāvaka another?"
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the signless one thing, and the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha another; is the signless one thing, and the dharmas of a bodhisattva another; is the signless one thing, and the dharmas of a buddha another?"
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"Is it not the case, Subhūti, that the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, the qualities of a bodhisattva, and the qualities of a buddha are all indeed signless?"
He said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Subhūti, by this method you should understand it thus:"
That is to say, all dharmas are signless (*animitta*). For in this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in all signless dharmas increases in wholesome dharmas;

namely, by means of the six perfections, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, and the five [faculties].
By means of the five faculties, the five powers, the six recollections, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and so on, up to all the qualities of a Buddha. For what reason?
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva has nothing else in which to train; he must train in no other than the dharmas that are empty, signless, and wishless. For what reason?

For within these three gates of liberation, all wholesome dharmas are included. That is to say: emptiness of intrinsic characteristics is the gate of liberation of emptiness; the departure from signs is the gate of liberation of the signless; and the absence of volitional formation is the gate of liberation of the wishless. (AdSPG II 65)
Training here in these three gates of liberation, that bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the five aggregates;
he trains in the twelve bases; he trains in the eighteen elements; he trains in the four noble truths;
he trains in the twelve-linked dependent origination; he trains in internal emptiness; [and] he trains in external emptiness.
He trains. He trains in internal-external emptiness; he trains up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

Likewise, he trains in the six perfections; he trains in the four foundations of mindfulness; he trains up to the noble eightfold path; he trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata; [he trains] in the four grounds of self-confidence and the four analytical knowledges.
He trains in great loving-kindness, in great compassion, and in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Subhūti said:
"But how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the five aggregates of clinging?"
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom thoroughly understands form. He understands how form arises, how form ceases, and what the suchness of form is. How does he thoroughly understand form?"
It is because of its extreme porosity and its extreme hollowness. He understands form to be just like a mass of foam, which is without essence. And how does he understand the arising of form?

He understands the arising of form through its coming from nowhere and its going nowhere—that is, by the fact that form does not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere. That which has not come from anywhere and has not gone anywhere—[that is the nature of form].

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands the arising and passing away of form. And how does he understand the suchness (*tathatā*) of form? Suchness neither arises nor ceases; it does not come nor go; it is neither defiled nor purified; it neither diminishes nor increases. It is in this way that he understands suchness. Subhūti, suchness is non-falsity.

Therefore, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*). It is not otherwise than that; thus it is called "suchness. In this way, one thoroughly understands the suchness of form. And how does one understand feeling?
How does one understand the arising of feeling, how the passing away of feeling, and how one thoroughly understands the suchness of feeling?
Just as water bubbles arise empty and cease empty, so too does one understand feeling:
it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. In this way, one understands the arising and passing away of feeling. And how does one understand the suchness of feeling?

It is the suchness of non-falsity. In this way, one understands the suchness of feeling. And how does one understand perception? It is just as water is absolutely not to be found in a mirage; in this way, one understands perception. It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; in this way, one understands the arising and passing away of perception. And how does one understand the suchness of perception?
Just as he understands the suchness of feeling, so too does he understand the suchness of perception. How does he understand formative forces (*saṃskāra*)?

It is just as, for example, the core of a plantain tree is found to be without core; even when one peels away leaf after leaf, nothing is obtained. In this way he understands formative forces. How does he understand the arising and passing away of formative forces?

One understands the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through their non-coming from anywhere and non-going anywhere. And how does one understand the suchness (*tathatā*) of conditioned phenomena?
One understands the suchness of conditioned phenomena through the suchness of feeling (*vedanā*). How does one understand consciousness (*vijñāna*)?
It is just as, for example, an army of four divisions created by a magician; in this way one understands consciousness. It is not [real].
It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. In this way, one understands the arising and passing away of consciousness. How does one understand the suchness (*tathatā*) of consciousness?
One understands the suchness of consciousness through the suchness of feeling. And how does one understand the elements (*dhātu*)?
The eye element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye element. The form element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the form element.

The eye-consciousness element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness element. In this manner, it should be applied up to the mind element, the phenomena element, and the mind-consciousness element. And how does one understand the sense bases?
Internal phenomena are empty of internal phenomena;
external phenomena are empty of external phenomena. In this way, one understands the sense bases (*āyatana*). And how does one understand the noble truths?
One understands suffering; one understands the truth; one understands the noble truth. It is free from duality.

He understands that the noble truth is indeed non-dual, for it is the truth of the noble ones. In this way, he understands the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path leading to cessation. How does he understand the suchness of suffering?
Suchness...

In this way, one understands the suchness (*tathatā*) of suffering; likewise, one understands the suchness of its origin, its cessation, and the path. And how does one understand dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?

One understands dependent origination from the standpoint of non-arising. Thus, one understands dependent origination as being without cessation, without annihilation, without permanence, without unity, without plurality, without coming, without going, and as the stilling of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)—that is, as peace.
In this way, one understands dependent origination.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, [perceives] these things as mutually distinct..."
One understands phenomena in this way. [Subhūti asked: "But, Blessed One, would not the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) then be disturbed?
The Blessed One said:
"It would be disturbed, Subhūti, if there were something else apart from the realm of phenomena."

There might be some dharma. But, Subhūti, no dharma other than the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is apprehended. If one were to be apprehended, there would be a disturbance of the dharma-realm. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, neither by the Tathāgata, nor by a Bodhisattva, nor by a Pratyekabuddha, nor by a Śrāvaka of the Tathāgata, has any dharma other than the dharma-realm ever been apprehended. Not having apprehended it...

He does not designate [any phenomenon], thinking that "some other phenomenon exists apart from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu). In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in the realm of phenomena.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), in what does he train?
The Blessed One replied:
“Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the realm of phenomena, he has trained in all phenomena. Why is that?”
For in this way, Subhūti, all phenomena are the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
He asked: "For what reason, Blessed One, are all phenomena the realm of phenomena?
The Blessed One replied:

For it is thus, Subhūti: whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, the *dharmadhātu* of phenomena remains established by way of its indivisibility. That is to say, the *dharmadhātu* consists of both the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) and the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*).
This should be applied in the same manner to all phenomena. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train].
"One who trains in the perfection of wisdom trains in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
He asked: "Blessed One, if all phenomena are the realm of phenomena, how then should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom?"
In what way should one train in the perfection of concentration, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity?
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the first dhyāna?
How should they train in the second, the third, and the fourth dhyānas?
How should one train in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; and from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
How should one train in the four applications of mindfulness up to the noble eightfold path? How should one train in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
How should one train in the eighteen liberations and the nine successive attainments?

How should one train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How should one train in the five supernormal knowledges?
How should one train in the perfection of the thirty-two marks of a great man? How should one train in the perfection of the eighty secondary characteristics?
How should one train for rebirth in a great kṣatriya clan, a great brāhmaṇa clan, or a great householder clan?

And how for rebirth among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, the Paranirmitavaśavartin, the Brahmakāyika, the Ābhāsvara, and the Śubhakṛtsna [heavens]?
Should one train for rebirth among the Vṛhaṇas, the Parīttavṛhaṇas, and the Bṛhatphala gods?

How should one train for rebirth among the non-percipient beings (asaṃjñisattva), and how for rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa host of gods? How should one train in the first production of the thought of awakening (prathama-cittotpāda)? How [should one train] in the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth?

One should train in the ninth and tenth productions of the thought of awakening. How should one train in the stage of the Śrāvaka, the stage of the Pratyekabuddha, and the fixed course of the Bodhisattva?
How should one train in the ripening of sentient beings, the purification of the Buddha-field, and in all the gateways of dhāraṇīs and gateways of samādhis?
How should one train in eloquence?
How should one train in the path to enlightenment, such that by training therein all phenomena are to be known in all their aspects?

If, Blessed One, these conceptual constructions do not exist within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), then, Blessed One, let it not be that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in perversion, and should proliferate that which is non-proliferated. Why is that?

For indeed, Blessed One, these conceptual constructions do not exist within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The dharma-realm is not form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations; the dharma-realm is not consciousness. The dharma-realm is not apart from form, nor apart from feeling, perception, or mental formations, nor apart from consciousness. Form itself is the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm is form.
Form is thus; up to consciousness, consciousness is the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm is consciousness. In this way, all dharmas are to be known.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is."

It is just as you say. Form itself is the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm itself is form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm itself is consciousness. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in the perfection of wisdom...

If one were to practice while perceiving any phenomenon as being separate from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), one would not be established in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Since all phenomena are the realm of phenomena, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom,
knowing all phenomena to be the realm of phenomena, teaches all nameless phenomena by means of names and conventions.
"This is form," "this is feeling," "this is perception," "these are mental formations," "this is consciousness," up to "this is awakening.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled magician or a magician’s apprentice were to produce whatever [illusion] it might be.

Having empowered a collection of substances, he can manifest various forms, namely: the form of an elephant, or the form of a horse, or the form of an ox, or the form of a man, woman, boy, or girl; or delightful parks, celestial palaces, groves, and gardens;
or delightful lotus ponds, or delightful forests.
Where there are various kinds of rugs, coverings, and spreadings; where he might display qualities such as flower garlands, or various kinds of food and drink;

or where he might delight the people with song and instrumental music; or while giving gifts, guarding ethical discipline, perfecting patience, exerting vigor, cultivating concentration, or developing wisdom—he should delight the people there by means of these modes.
He might show him great kṣatriya clans, or great brahmin clans, or great householder clans; or he might show him the gods of the Four Great Kings,

or Mount Sumeru, or the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, or the Paranirmitavaśavartin, up to and including the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

[He does not perceive] formless stream-enterers, or once-returners, or non-returners, or arhats, or pratyekabuddhas; nor even those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, from the first production of the thought of awakening, practice the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline,
the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.

They practice. They practice on the first stage, up to practicing on the tenth great stage. They enter the fixed course of the bodhisattvas and manifest the superknowledges (*abhijñā*). With those superknowledges they sport and bring sentient beings to maturity. And they purify the buddha-field by means of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*).

They sport; or they relinquish their limbs and members; or they practice difficult austerities; or they bring to perfection the powers of a Tathāgata; or they manifest the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, or great compassion—they should display all these as well. Or they should manifest the body of a Buddha, complete with all its major and minor limbs. Therein, those of the nature of fools—
Beings would think thus:

"Aha! How well-trained is this man; how skillfully he acts! For he delights these people in this way and displays such various forms, even up to the form of a Buddha. Furthermore, those who were there...

There are men who are wise, discerning, and intelligent, endowed with such an investigation that they think to themselves: "This is wonderful, this is a marvelous phenomenon; yet herein no phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended. And yet this man delights this multitude with such non-existent phenomena, while he himself does not apprehend that notion of a 'being'."

"These beings, who perceive what is not a substantial entity as a substantial entity"— in this very way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom with skillful means, does not see any phenomenon as being separate from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); nor does he apprehend a sentient being, nor even the designation "sentient being."
(VIII 5,5) He himself gives gifts and encourages others to give gifts; he speaks in praise of giving and approves of those other beings who also give gifts.
He himself maintains ethical discipline and encourages others to maintain ethical discipline; he speaks in praise of ethical discipline and [approves of those who do so].

Others also guard their ethical discipline; he speaks in praise of them and approves of them. Likewise, he himself cultivates patience and encourages others to undertake patience. He speaks in praise of patience; others who cultivate patience, he also speaks in praise of them and approves of them. And he himself [exerts] vigor...

He exerts himself; he encourages others to undertake vigor and speaks in praise of vigor. He is one who speaks in praise of and approves of those others who also exert vigor. He enters into meditative absorption himself and encourages others to enter into meditative absorption. He speaks in praise of meditative absorption and [approves] those others who also enter into meditative absorption.

And he speaks in praise of them and approves of them. He himself cultivates wisdom, encourages others to undertake wisdom, speaks in praise of wisdom, and approves of those others who also cultivate wisdom. He speaks in their praise and gives his approval.

(VIII 5,6) They themselves undertake and abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, and they encourage others to undertake the ten paths of wholesome action. They also speak in praise of the ten paths of wholesome action.
As for those others... (AdSPG II 71)
Sentient beings undertake and abide by the ten paths of wholesome action, and he speaks in praise of them and approves of them.
He himself observes the *poṣadha* endowed with the eight limbs, and he encourages others to undertake the *poṣadha* endowed with the eight limbs;
he speaks in praise of the *poṣadha* endowed with the eight limbs. And as for other sentient beings who [observe] the *poṣadha* endowed with the eight limbs...
They observe the *poṣadha*. He speaks in praise of them and approves of them. Being joyful himself, he undertakes and abides by the five precepts;
he encourages others to undertake the five precepts and speaks in praise of the five precepts. Furthermore, he speaks in praise of those other beings who undertake and abide by the five precepts.

He becomes one who gives his consent. Thus, he himself enters the first dhyāna up to the fourth; he practices loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; he enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite space up to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He himself cultivates the foundations of mindfulness up to the noble eightfold path and the three gateways to liberation.
He cultivates the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges,

great loving-kindness, great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the eighty minor marks. Furthermore, he encourages others to undertake the eighty minor marks and speaks in praise of the eighty minor marks.
He speaks in praise of and approves of those other beings who cultivate the eighty secondary marks.
(VIII 5,7) Subhūti, if the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) were not as it was before, as it is after, and as it is in the middle,
then the bodhisattva mahāsattva would not, through skill in means, indicate the realm of phenomena to sentient beings, nor [would he guide] sentient beings...

And he will bring them to maturity. For this reason, Subhūti, because the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is the same in the beginning, the same in the end, and the same in the middle, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom indicates the realm of phenomena to sentient beings through skillful means. For the sake of sentient beings, he practices the conduct of a bodhisattva and brings sentient beings to maturity.
// The Chapter on the Exposition of the Equality of All Dharmas. // 74 //
Chapter 75: The Exposition on the Unshakable.
Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, if a sentient being is ultimately not apprehended,"
"If there is no designation of a 'being,' for what purpose does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the perfection of wisdom?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

Subhūti, it is by taking the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as the standard that a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, if the limit of reality were one thing and the limit of sentient beings (*sattvakoṭi*) another, then a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not course in the perfection of wisdom. But since, Subhūti, the limit of reality is not one thing and the limit of sentient beings another, therefore a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of sentient beings. In the perfection of wisdom...
“Subhūti, while practicing, a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes beings in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) by way of not disturbing the limit of reality.
He asked: “Blessed One, if the limit of reality is the limit of beings, then how does the limit of reality establish [beings] in the limit of reality?”

If, Blessed One, the limit of reality were to abide in the limit of reality, then intrinsic nature would abide in intrinsic nature. But, Blessed One, intrinsic nature does not abide in intrinsic nature.
How then, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, establish sentient beings in the limit of reality?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, the limit of reality does not abide in the limit of reality; intrinsic nature does not abide in intrinsic nature.
Nevertheless, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful means..."
One establishes the limit of sentient beings (*sattvakoṭi*) in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Yet, the limit of reality is not other than the limit of sentient beings;
for indeed, the limit of sentient beings and the limit of reality are non-dual, an indivisible unity.
He asked: "O Blessed One, what is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, by which skillful means..."
"Endowed with what does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, establish beings in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) without disturbing the limit of reality?
The Blessed One said:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, from the first production of the thought of awakening, establishes sentient beings in generosity. Having established them in generosity, he explains to them the prior limit, the later limit, and the middle of that generosity. Just as that generosity is empty of a prior limit, empty of a later limit, and empty of a middle, so too [is it empty].

In the same way, the fruit of giving is empty; the donor is empty; the recipient is also empty. Thus, noble son, all these things do not exist within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Do not conceive of the gift as one thing and the fruit of the gift as another;
do not conceive of the donor as one thing and the recipient as another. When you, noble son, [do not perceive them] as distinct...

You will regard the gift as one thing and the fruit of the gift as another; you will regard the donor as one thing and the recipient as another. Then this gift of yours will become the deathless (*amṛta*), culminating in the deathless fruit.
And by means of this gift, do not grasp at form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness. Why is that?

For just as this gift is empty of a gift, its fruit is empty of a fruit, the giver of the gift is empty of a giver of the gift, and the recipient is empty of a recipient—so too, in emptiness, no gift is apprehended; neither the fruit of the gift, nor the giver of the gift, nor the recipient is apprehended. Why is that?
Because these phenomena are, by their very nature, ultimately empty. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, through skill in means establishes beings in ethical discipline. He says:

"Come, son of good family, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from the taking of life; and so on, until: having abandoned wrong view, abstain from wrong view. Son of good family, not even the slightest intrinsic nature exists in these phenomena."
Just as you have imagined it,
come now, noble son, investigate this:
which is this phenomenon of "living beings" that you will deprive of life, or by what means will you deprive them?

...up to what must be done regarding wrong view. And, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with this skill in means, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, brings sentient beings to maturity. He explains to them the fruit of that giving and the fruit of that morality; yet even that fruit of giving and the fruit of morality are empty of intrinsic nature. Then he—
Having understood that the fruit of giving and morality is empty, the son of good family does not become attached to it.

Not becoming attached, he gives rise to non-distraction and thereby produces wisdom. By means of that wisdom, having severed all latent tendencies and active defilements, he attains final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder. This is according to worldly convention, but not according to ultimate truth.
For what reason?
Because in emptiness no phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended, whether it be one that attains parinirvāṇa or one that has been brought to parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, his very parinirvāṇa is indeed absolute emptiness (*atyantaśūnyatā*). Moreover—

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees other beings and other persons who are agitated and possessed of malicious intent, he instructs them thus and exhorts them thus: "Come, noble son, accomplish patience and cultivate patience."
Be of a nature that endures,
whether it be the one who becomes angry, that by which one becomes angry, or that toward which one becomes angry;
for all these phenomena are empty by their very nature.
Come now, noble son, investigate this: who is it that becomes angry here? Toward what is one angry? Or by what means is one angry?
All these phenomena are empty by nature. And that which is emptiness by nature is never non-empty;
it was not made by the Tathāgatas, nor by Pratyekabuddhas, nor by Śrāvakas, nor by Bodhisattvas, nor by gods.

Neither by the nāgas, nor by the yakṣas, nor by the gandharvas, nor by the kinnaras, nor by the mahoragas, nor by the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm, up to and including the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods; neither by the Brahmās, up to and including the Śubhakṛtsna gods, nor by the Śuddhāvāsa gods, up to and including the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Therefore, come now, noble son!
Examine this thoroughly: who here is being harmed? Or toward whom am I being harmed? Or by what am I being harmed?

All these phenomena are empty by nature. For emptiness does not harbor malice toward anyone. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, [establishes] beings in the emptiness of intrinsic nature through skillful means.

He engages them both in the cause and in the fruit. Engaging them in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, he gradually inspires, encourages, settles, and establishes them in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Yet this is according to worldly convention, and not according to the ultimate truth. Why is that?

For in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is nothing whatsoever that could attain, nor anything by which one might attain, nor anything that could be attained. Subhūti, this limit of reality is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, wherein the bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of sentient beings.
And therein he does not perceive a sentient being, nor the designation "sentient being. Why is that?

Because all phenomena are indeed secluded from a sentient being. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom perceives through skillful means sentient beings who are of inferior energy and indolent, [he inspires them] thus in physical and mental vigor.

He encourages them. For, noble son, in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), there is no sinking down of any dharma whatsoever. That in which one might sink, that by which one might sink, or he who might sink—all these dharmas do not transcend the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Therefore, come now! Having generated physical and mental vigor and having cast off laziness, [apply yourselves] to wholesome dharmas.
Whether it be in generosity, or in ethical discipline, or in patience, or in vigor; whether it be in meditative concentration, or in wisdom;
whether it be in the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; or in the applications of mindfulness, or up to the noble eightfold path; or in emptiness, or...
Whether it be the signless, or the wishless,
or all the qualities of a Buddha:
O son of good family, behold all these phenomena as unobstructed through emptiness.

For there is no sinking whatsoever of any dharma among dharmas that are unobstructed. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, through skill in means, encourages beings in intrinsic emptiness, settles them in it, and establishes them in it; he establishes them further in such a way that—
Duality does not exist. For what reason?
Because intrinsic emptiness is non-dual and undivided; for a non-dual phenomenon does not sink into anything. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva...

Practicing the perfection of wisdom, he instructs and exhorts beings toward vigor by means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature: "Come, son of good family, exert vigor! Whether it be in generosity, or in ethical discipline, or in patience;
whether it be in vigor, or in meditative concentration, or in wisdom; whether it be in the applications of mindfulness, or even up to the noble eightfold path."

On the path; whether it be in the eight liberations, or in the nine successive attainments; whether it be in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, or in the four grounds of self-confidence; whether it be in the four analytical knowledges, or in great loving-kindness, or in great compassion, or in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Do not attend to these phenomena as dual, nor as non-dual;
for what reason?
These phenomena are empty by their very nature.

Furthermore, the emptiness of intrinsic nature should not be attended to as dual, nor as non-dual. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom through skillful means performs the conduct of a bodhisattva and brings sentient beings to maturity. Having brought sentient beings to maturity, he gradually establishes them in the fruit of stream-entry and in the fruit of once-returning.

He establishes them in the fruit of non-returning, in arhatship, in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and even in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, through skill in means,
instructs and exhorts sentient beings with distracted minds as follows:
Come, son of good family, cultivate samādhi;
do not have the notion of distraction, nor the notion of samādhi. Why is that?
Because these phenomena are empty by nature.
Furthermore, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), no phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended that is either distracted or becomes one-pointed.

Therefore, abiding in this samādhi, whatever root of virtue you shall perform—whether by body, speech, or mind; whether you shall give a gift, or guard your ethical discipline, or accomplish yourself through patience.

Whether you will exert vigor, or produce meditative concentration, or cultivate wisdom; whether you will practice the applications of mindfulness, or [practice] up to the noble eightfold path; or whether [you will practice] the three gateways to liberation, or the eight liberations.
Whether it be in the nine successive attainments; or in the ten powers of a Tathāgata; or in the four grounds of self-confidence; or in the four analytical knowledges;
or in great loving-kindness, or in great compassion, great sympathetic joy, or great equanimity; or in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Whether it be in the thirty-two marks of a great man, or in the eighty secondary characteristics; whether it be in the path of the śrāvaka, or in the path of the pratyekabuddha, or in the path of the bodhisattva, or in the path of the Buddha; whether it be in the fruit of stream-entry, or in the fruit of once-returning, or in the fruit of non-returning, or in arhatship.
Whether it be toward individual enlightenment, or toward the knowledge of all aspects, or toward the ripening of sentient beings, or toward the purification of a Buddha-field—
these wholesome qualities will appear to you with little difficulty as you course in the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom performs the welfare of sentient beings through skill in means;

from the first production of the thought of awakening, he is never without activity. Seeking what is wholesome, he performs the welfare of sentient beings and constantly and continuously travels from buddhafield to buddhafield, attending upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

Furthermore, whatever Dharma he hears from those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, it never perishes for him even after he has passed through a change of birth, until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. He becomes one who has constantly and perpetually attained *dhāraṇī*, with his faculties unimpaired— whether by means of the faculty of body or the faculty of speech.
Or perhaps by means of the mind-faculty. Why is that?
Because omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) has been constantly and continuously well-cultivated;
therefore, by means of this well-cultivated omniscience, all paths become well-cultivated.
Whether it be the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the bodhisattva,
the superknowledges (abhijñā) of that bodhisattva mahāsattva become a constant and continuous benefit to him through the principle of non-dissipation.
Abiding in those superknowledges born of karmic maturation, he acts for the welfare of sentient beings, and he does not fall away from the five realms of existence.
Wandering in saṃsāra, Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

practicing the perfection of wisdom and established in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), works for the benefit of sentient beings through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). With that well-cultivated perfection of wisdom, he thus instructs and thus advises sentient beings.
He instructs him: "Come, son of good family, whatever action you perform—whether by body, speech, or mind—contemplate all of that as being empty of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnya*).

In this way, all your actions will have the fruit of immortality (*amṛta-phala*) and will culminate in immortality. Furthermore, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, no phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended that could either perish or decline."
For what reason?
Because intrinsic emptiness does not diminish, nor does any phenomenon diminish within intrinsic emptiness. For what reason?
Because intrinsic emptiness is neither an entity nor a non-entity. How, then, could there be any diminution among phenomena whose intrinsic nature is non-existence?

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom instructs and exhorts sentient beings through skillful means. Instructing and exhorting in this manner, he never becomes inactive. He himself constantly and continuously abides in the ten paths of wholesome action, and [he establishes] others in the ten paths of wholesome action as well.

He encourages others to undertake the paths of action. Likewise, he himself undertakes the five precepts and the eightfold fast, and he encourages others to do the same. He himself enters the first dhyāna and encourages others to enter the first dhyāna; likewise, up to the fourth dhyāna. He himself dwells constantly and continuously in loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and encourages others to dwell constantly and continuously in it.

He encourages others to cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Likewise, he encourages them in compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), up to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samāpatti*). He himself cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and encourages others in the foundations of mindfulness. Likewise, up to the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). He himself trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata (*daśatathāgatabala*) and [encourages] others in the ten...

He encourages others in the powers of a Tathāgata; he establishes them, disciplines them, and settles them therein. Likewise, up to the eighty secondary marks, he himself produces the knowledge of the fruit of stream-entry, yet he does not abide therein, and he establishes others in the fruit of stream-entry. Likewise, up to arhatship and pratyekabodhi, he himself [produces] the unsurpassed...

He generates the path to perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, he speaks of that path, instructs others, establishes them in it, disciplines them, and settles them therein. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom through skillful means never fails to perform his work.
He said: "If, Blessed One, all phenomena are empty by nature, and within this emptiness of nature neither a sentient being is perceived,
nor a phenomenon, nor a non-phenomenon,
then how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva establish himself for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects?"
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is; it is just as you say."
All phenomena are empty by nature;
and within this emptiness of nature, no sentient being is apprehended,
neither dharma nor non-dharma.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if all phenomena were not empty by nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not abide in the emptiness of nature. Having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he would not teach that phenomena are empty by nature. Subhūti, form is empty by nature.

Subhūti, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty by nature. Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, teaches the Dharma that the five aggregates are empty by nature. He teaches the Dharma that the eighteen elements and the twelve sense bases are empty by nature. [He teaches] the four meditative absorptions, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments...

He teaches the Dharma that the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the noble eightfold path, are empty by nature; likewise the three gateways to liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities.

He teaches the Dharma that the Buddha-qualities— the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics— are empty by nature. He teaches the Dharma that the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, individual enlightenment, omniscience, and the abandonment of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies are empty by nature.

He teaches. Furthermore, Subhūti, if internal emptiness were not empty by nature, the bodhisattva mahāsattva would not teach the Dharma that all phenomena are empty by nature. Likewise, [he would not teach] external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, and the emptiness of the unconditioned.
Would absolute emptiness, beginningless and endless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of all phenomena,
and emptiness of specific characteristics not be empty of intrinsic nature? For that would mean their intrinsic nature is subject to destruction.
And intrinsic emptiness does not perish; it does not become immutable, nor does it ever return. Why is that?
Because it is neither situated in a place nor situated in a location;
indeed, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. This is the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), wherein nothing whatsoever [is established].

Neither an accumulation nor a depletion of phenomena is perceived; neither loss nor increase, neither arising nor cessation, neither defilement nor purification. This is that very nature of phenomena, abiding in which bodhisattva mahāsattvas establish themselves for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; and yet, there is not even the slightest phenomenon [that exists].

He perceives setting forth, but not non-setting forth. For all phenomena are neither set forth nor established; this is the established nature of phenomena (*dharmasthitatā*). Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), seeing that all phenomena are empty by nature, he does not turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Why is that?

For he does not perceive the obscuration of any dharma whatsoever; he perceives all dharmas as unobscured. Why then would he have doubt regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—in that intrinsic emptiness where no sentient being is apprehended, nor the designation of a sentient being, nor a self, nor a living soul, nor a nourisher, nor a person, nor a creature?

Neither a human being, nor a person, nor an agent, nor one who causes to act, nor an experiencer, nor one who causes experience, nor an arouser, nor a producer, nor a seer is apprehended. Neither form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness is apprehended.
In this way, internal and external phenomena are to be treated, up to the eighty secondary marks.
(VIII 5,8) "Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, an emanation of the Tathāgata were to teach the Dharma continuously for ten million eons to an emanated monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman.

What do you think, Subhūti: would those emanations be capable of attaining the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or pratyekabuddhahood, or even of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. And why is that?
Because for them, there is no objective basis.
The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. Since all dharmas are without substance, what sentient being is there whom a bodhisattva mahāsattva could establish in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or in arhatship, or in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"

Elsewhere, wisdom that is bound by perversion establishes and settles [beings] in non-perversion. That which is perversion is itself non-perversion, based on the outflow of conceptual construction (*kalpaniṣyanda*). Non-conceptualization is non-perversion;
where there is no perversion, there is no self, no sentient being, and so forth, up to no agent and no perceiver.
In that state, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness, up to and including no awakening;

wherein there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness, up to and including no awakening—this is that emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Abiding in this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

He liberates beings from their perversion regarding the notion of a "being. In this way, he liberates them from the notion of form and from the notion of the formless, and so on, until he liberates them from all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
Even those phenomena that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), such as the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

The four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the three gateways to liberation, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—
even those are not the ultimate truth in that manner.
That is to say: the unconditioned, non-arising, non-existence, and non-manifestation—this is that emptiness of intrinsic nature;
this is the awakening of the Blessed Buddhas, wherein there is no sentient being, and so on, up to no progenitor and no beholder.

It is not form, not feeling, not perception, not mental formations, and not consciousness. This should be applied in detail, up to the eighty secondary marks. For it is not for the sake of a path that the bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; rather, it is for the purpose of fully understanding intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). That intrinsic emptiness, moreover, was [previously...]
Whether it is that intrinsic emptiness at the beginning,
or that intrinsic emptiness at the end, or that intrinsic emptiness in the middle,
it is never not intrinsic emptiness. Therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the perfections of intrinsic emptiness—
Moving for the sake of liberating all perceptions of those beings who possess the perception of a "being," he courses in the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).

Coursing in that knowledge of the aspects of the path, he courses in all paths—namely, the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the bodhisattva. Furthermore, having fully perfected all paths, that bodhisattva mahāsattva [liberates] sentient beings...

Having ripened the buddha-field and purified it, and having empowered his life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. He does not interrupt the lineage of the Buddhas—that is to say, the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). This is that lineage of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

Those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who existed in the past, for those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, this was the guidance of a Buddha, namely, intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who will exist in the future, for those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, this will be the guidance of a Buddha, namely, intrinsic emptiness;
and those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who currently reside, stay, and maintain themselves in the world-systems in the ten directions.
For those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, this is the guidance of the Buddha, namely, intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*).
Indeed, the manifestation of intrinsic emptiness in the world does not occur from any source other than in the presence of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
likewise, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfections of intrinsic emptiness.
Wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing, does not fall away from omniscience.
Subhūti said:

"O Blessed One, this is marvelous regarding the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, that they indeed course in all phenomena which are empty by nature (*prakṛti-śūnya*). And yet, they do not disturb that emptiness of nature, [thinking] that form is one thing and the emptiness of nature another; likewise, that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are one thing and the emptiness of nature another. This should be applied extensively to all phenomena, up to the point where awakening is one thing and the emptiness of nature is another."

Form itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature itself is form; feeling itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature itself is feeling; perception itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature itself is perception;
mental formations themselves are the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature itself is mental formations.

Consciousness itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature itself is consciousness. Likewise, up to awakening itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature itself is awakening.
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, if form were one thing and the emptiness of intrinsic nature another; if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were one thing [and the emptiness of intrinsic nature another]..."

There would be one thing that is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and another that is awakening, and yet another that is the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Subhūti, if form were not empty of intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. It is the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations.

If consciousness were not empty by nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and if awakening were not empty by nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, Subhūti, because form is empty by nature, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty by nature, [a bodhisattva realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment].
Up to enlightenment, [all things] are empty by nature;
therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having understood that all phenomena are empty by nature, awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?
Because herein no phenomenon whatsoever perishes, nor does it remain immutable, nor does it enter [into existence].

Otherwise, the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās would be deluded, thinking: "This is form; I am form; form is mine," and so on up to: "This is consciousness; I am consciousness; consciousness is mine.

Having become attached to form and so on up to consciousness, they course in the notions of "I" and "mine. Having become attached to the notions of "I" and "mine," they become attached to internal and external entities.
Having become attached and having been reborn, they grasp at the sense-bases: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
They are not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
they are not liberated from the saṃsāra of the five destinies.

Thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfections of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, he does not disturb form, thinking "it is empty" or "it is not empty. He does not disturb feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, thinking "it is empty" or "it is not empty. He does not disturb even awakening, thinking "it is empty" or "it is not empty. Why is that? Because the emptiness of form does not disturb form. This is form; this is the emptiness of form. And so on, up to: this is consciousness.

This is the emptiness of consciousness, up to and including this awakening and the emptiness of awakening. Subhūti, it is just as space does not disturb space; internal space does not disturb external space, nor does external space disturb internal space. In the same way, Subhūti, form does not disturb emptiness.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not disturb emptiness; emptiness does not disturb consciousness. Likewise, awakening does not disturb emptiness; emptiness does not disturb awakening. Why is that? Because these have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that could thus be disturbed. This is form, this is emptiness; this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is emptiness; and so on, up to: this is awakening, this is emptiness.
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, all dharmas are without differentiation,
from where has the bodhisattva mahāsattva set out, thinking, 'I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment'?"
“Moreover, Blessed One, awakening is not a state of duality, nor is it possible for one who acts with duality to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
The Blessed One said:
“So it is, Subhūti; so it is.”
Enlightenment does not course in duality, nor is enlightenment a state of bifurcation;

for, Subhūti, enlightenment is non-dual and free from bifurcation. Enlightenment, Subhūti, does not course in the bifurcation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva as "enlightenment"—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva.

Or rather: that awakening of the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not course in form; it does not course in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor does it course in awakening itself. Why is that?
Because awakening is neither "I" nor "mine."
"I would course in form; form is mine.
