By means of those superknowledges, he performs those tasks that are to be accomplished through superknowledge. In this regard, the bodhisattva mahāsattva...

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees the world-systems in the eastern direction, the southern, the western, the northern, the nadir, the intermediate directions, above, and across. Having gone there by means of his supernatural power, he works for the benefit of sentient beings.

He practices: whether by means of giving, or morality, or patience, or vigor, or concentration, or wisdom; or by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; or by means of the meditative absorptions, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, and the meditative equipoises;
or by means of the dharmas of the śrāvakas, or the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, or the dharmas of the bodhisattvas.

Or else, he acts for the benefit of those beings by means of the Buddha-dharmas. In that regard, to those beings who are stingy, he teaches the Dharma thus: "Give gifts, for poverty is indeed suffering."
For by poverty it is not possible even to accomplish one's own welfare, much less that of another;
thus you will suffer yourselves and cause others to suffer.
Do not, overcome by poverty, devour one another's flesh and fail to be liberated from the three lower realms.
To those beings who are immoral, he teaches the Dharma in this way: "O men, immorality is indeed suffering.
For one who is immoral is not even able to accomplish his own welfare, let alone that of another. The ripening of immorality is either rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama."
Therefore, you have fallen into the three miserable destinies; you are not even able to accomplish your own welfare, let alone that of others.
Thus, you must not allow even a single moment of an immoral mind to arise, lest you later come to regret it. To those beings who harbor malice toward one another, he teaches the Dharma in this way.

Do not harbor malice toward one another. For those whose minds are agitated, no wholesome quality whatsoever can arise; since your minds are thus mutually agitated, it is possible that you may be reborn in hell, or in the animal realm, or in the world of Yama. Therefore, alas, you must not allow even a single thought to become disturbed.
Much less should any opportunity be given to other unwholesome states of mind. Those who are lazy he enjoins to vigor;
likewise, up to those whose minds are distracted, he enjoins them to meditative concentration; those who lack wisdom, he enjoins to wisdom;
those whose conduct is dominated by passion, he enjoins to the meditation on the foul; and those whose conduct is dominated by hatred, he enjoins to loving-kindness.

He applies them. Those whose conduct is dominated by delusion, he applies to dependent origination. Those who have set out upon wrong paths, he applies to the path—whether he applies them to the path of the śrāvaka or to the path of the pratyekabuddha. To them he teaches the Dharma in this way:
Those phenomena to which you are attached are empty of intrinsic nature;

for it is not possible to be attached to phenomena that are empty of intrinsic nature. And emptiness is itself unattached. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, [proceeds].

Abiding in the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), he works for the benefit of sentient beings. Subhūti, there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva who is able to teach the Dharma to sentient beings without abiding in the superknowledges, nor is it possible for him to lead sentient beings who have set out on a wrong path onto the right path; such a thing is impossible. Subhūti, just as a winged bird cannot traverse the sky if it is without wings, even so, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva—

Without having attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), one is not able to teach the Dharma. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) should bring forth the superknowledges. By means of these superknowledges thus brought forth, he will accomplish whatever he desires for the benefit of sentient beings and will bring them happiness.

With the divine eye, he will see world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā. He will see the beings born there. Having seen those beings, he will go to them by means of his supernatural power and, with his own mind, discern their minds;
having discerned them, he will teach the Dharma accordingly—whether it be a discourse on giving, or indeed any discourse leading to liberation.
Regarding this discourse: with the divine ear-element, he will hear both kinds of sounds—namely, those that are divine and those that are human.

Therein, as for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who in the eastern direction, and so on, throughout the ten directions in every single direction, teach the Dharma in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—he, by means of that divine ear-element, [will hear] them.

He will hear the teachings; having heard them, he will grasp them for the sake of suchness. Having grasped them for the sake of suchness, he will teach the Dharma without deviation from suchness—ranging from discourses on giving to discourses on liberation. His knowledge of the mental dispositions of others will become utterly pure. By means of that knowledge of the mental dispositions of others, he will discern the minds of sentient beings.

He will teach the Dharma for their sake in accordance with reality—discourses on generosity, up to discourses on the way of deliverance. He will recollect his manifold past abodes, both his own and those of others. By means of that knowledge of recollecting past abodes, he will know thus: "Those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, together with their disciples, had such names."

There, to those beings who will be inclined toward the recollection of past lives, he will teach the Dharma for the sake of their realization of suchness—ranging from discourses on generosity up to discourses on liberation. Having traveled by means of his supernormal power to many various world-systems, he will attend upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; and having attended upon them, he will teach the Dharma to beings through his higher knowledge.

He will teach—discourses on giving, up to discourses on the way out [of suffering]. With his well-understood knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, he will teach the Dharma to sentient beings, whether it be a discourse on giving or a discourse on the way out. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train] in the perfection of wisdom.

One who is devoted [to this practice] should bring forth the superknowledges (*abhijñā*). When these superknowledges have been thoroughly mastered, whatever kind of personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) he may desire to assume, that very kind of personal existence he will assume. He will neither be elated by pleasure nor dejected by suffering; indeed, he will have no attachment or aversion whatsoever.

It is just as, for example, a person created by a Tathāgata performs all tasks and is not afflicted by either pleasure or pain. In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should sport with the superknowledges (abhijñā), so that while sporting, he will purify a buddha-field.

And he will bring sentient beings to maturity. Furthermore, Subhūti, it is not possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening if the buddha-field has not been purified and sentient beings have not been brought to maturity. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, there is no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is deficient in the factors of the path.
(VIII 5,19) Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

“Blessed One, what are the factors of the path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by fulfilling which a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? When this had been said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, all wholesome dharmas are the limbs of the path for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti asked: "But, Blessed One, what are those wholesome dharmas that are the limbs of the path, by means of which one fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One replied:

Starting from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, the perfection of giving is a wholesome dharma; therein, "non-conceptualization" means that while giving, one does not conceptualize. One does not conceptualize these three: "This is the gift," "I am giving this to him," or "I am the giver. Based on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, by means of this perfection, one crosses over oneself and causes others to cross over from the ocean of saṃsāra. These are those wholesome dharmas.

The path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva for the sake of unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening is that path by which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present have crossed, are crossing, and will cross over the ocean of saṃsāra. Thus it is with the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of wisdom, the four dhyānas, and the four immeasurables.
The four formless attainments; the four foundations of mindfulness; the four right efforts; the four bases of miraculous power;
the five faculties; the five powers; the seven factors of enlightenment; the noble eightfold path; the three gateways to liberation;
the fourteen kinds of emptiness; the eight liberations; the nine successive attainments; the gateways of dhāraṇī; and the gateways of samādhi.

The analytical knowledges, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—whatever constitutes the paths to enlightenment, these are the wholesome dharmas that must be fulfilled by a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
having fulfilled them, he attains all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Having attained it, he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Chapter 79 (VIII 5,20). Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"If, Blessed One, these dharmas are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, then what, moreover, are the dharmas of a Buddha?"
The Blessed One said:

"Furthermore, Subhūti, as to what you have said: 'If these dharmas are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, then what are the dharmas of a Buddha? Subhūti, these very same dharmas are the dharmas of a Buddha when one fully awakens to them in all their aspects."
For one who has attained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), every continuity of latent predispositions (*vāsanānusandhi*) is abandoned;
that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva fully awakens to this,
and that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has fully awakened to all phenomena through a wisdom endowed with the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).

This is the distinction between a bodhisattva and a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha. Subhūti, it is just as if one person were the one who has entered the path and another were the one who has attained the fruit; although they are both noble persons (*āryapudgala*), they are not the same.
Even so, Subhūti, [is the distinction between the bodhisattva and the Tathāgata].
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who has entered the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
whereas the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained the state of being free from darkness regarding all phenomena.
Subhūti, this is the distinction between the bodhisattva mahāsattva and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

"If, Blessed One, these dharmas are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), then within dharmas that are empty of their own specific characteristics, how can any distinction or differentiation be perceived?"

"This one belongs to the hells; this one belongs to the animal realm; this one belongs to the world of Yama; this one is a god; this one is a human; this one is a member of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhū*);

this one is an eighth-rank practitioner (*aṣṭamaka*); this one is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*); this one is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*); this one is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*); this one is an arhat; this one is a pratyekabuddha;
this one is a bodhisattva; this one is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Just as it is, Blessed One, with these persons...

They are not apprehended. It is just so, Blessed One; action is not apprehended. Just as action is not apprehended, so too the ripening of action is not apprehended. When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"So it is, Subhūti; so it is, just as you say. Within phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), neither action nor its maturation (*vipāka*) is apprehended. However, Subhūti, those who do not know phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics perform actions—whether misconduct or good conduct, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*). Through such misconduct..."

By [unwholesome] action they fall into the three lower realms; by good conduct they are reborn among gods and humans; and by flawless action they are reborn in the realm of form or the formless realm. Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of generosity, and so on up to practicing the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, practices these bodhisattva-dharmas with flawless conduct.

He generates them. Having generated them, he enters the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) accompanied by the retinue of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and thereby awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Having awakened, he effects the welfare of sentient beings.
That welfare, once effected, does not perish again; for were it to perish, one would fall back into the saṃsāra of the five destinies.
He asked: "Furthermore, after the Blessed One had fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, was the saṃsāra of the five destinies perceived?
The Blessed One said: "No.
He asked: "Furthermore, were black, white, or neither-black-nor-white phenomena perceived by the Tathāgata?"
The Blessed One said: "No.
He asked: "If they are not apprehended, from where are the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama designated? From where are gods and humans?"
From where are the designations "stream-enterer," "once-returner," "non-returner," "arhat," "pratyekabuddha," "bodhisattva," and "tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened one" derived?
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, do these beings know that all dharmas are empty of their own specific characteristics?
He replied, "No indeed.
The Blessed One said:

Furthermore, Subhūti, if sentient beings were to know that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), then the bodhisattva mahāsattva, not abiding in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, would not liberate sentient beings from the three lower realms up to the various states of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra-gati*). But because, Subhūti, sentient beings do not know that [phenomena] are empty of their own specific characteristics...

Not understanding these phenomena, they are not liberated from the saṃsāra of the five destinies. Therefore, having heard from those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, that all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes himself in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings. These phenomena do not exist in the way that [they appear].
Foolish ordinary people are attached; thus these beings, having themselves conceptualized and apprehended phenomena that are non-existent and not found,

perceive existence where there is no existence, the notion of form where there is no form, the notion of feeling where there is no feeling, and [the notion of perception] where there is no perception.
Perceiving what is not perception as perception, perceiving the unconditioned as conditioned, and perceiving what is not consciousness as consciousness—
up to the point that they conceptualize unconditioned phenomena as being non-existent and non-occurrent—
they, with minds inverted by these perversions, perform actions through body, speech, and mind. They [are bound] to the five destinies...

They are not liberated from cyclic existence. Therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, gathers all wholesome qualities within it and undertakes the conduct of a bodhisattva; by undertaking that conduct, he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

(VIII 5,21). Having fully awakened to suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering, he explains, teaches, makes known, establishes, reveals, analyzes, clarifies, and fully illuminates them.
Within those four noble truths, all wholesome qualities whatsoever are included—namely, all the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ*) by which...
The establishment of the Three Jewels occurs through the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*). Which three?
The Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
Through the manifestation of these Three Jewels, sentient beings are liberated from the saṃsāra of the five destinies.
Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

"Furthermore, Blessed One, does one attain parinirvāṇa through the knowledge of suffering, or through suffering itself? Does one attain parinirvāṇa through the knowledge of the origin [of suffering], or through the origin itself?"

"Is parinirvāṇa attained through the knowledge of the cessation of suffering, or through the cessation of suffering itself? Is parinirvāṇa attained through the knowledge of the path, or through the path itself? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Subhūti, parinirvāṇa does not occur through the knowledge of suffering, nor through suffering;

parinirvāṇa does not occur through the knowledge of the origin [of suffering], nor through the origin. Parinirvāṇa does not occur through the knowledge of the cessation of suffering, nor through the cessation of suffering. Parinirvāṇa does not occur through the knowledge of the path, nor through the path. That which...

Furthermore, Subhūti, I have declared that the equality of the four noble truths is parinirvāṇa; yet parinirvāṇa does not occur through the knowledge of suffering, nor through suffering itself, nor through the knowledge of the origin, nor through the origin itself, nor through the knowledge of the cessation of suffering, nor through the cessation of suffering itself, nor through the knowledge of the path, nor through the path itself.
He asked: "Lord, what is the sameness of these four noble truths?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, it is that wherein there is no suffering, no knowledge of suffering; no origin, no knowledge of the origin; no cessation..."

There is no knowledge of cessation, no path, and no knowledge of the path. That which is the suchness (*tathatā*), the non-falsity (*avitathatā*), the true nature (*dharmatā*) of these four noble truths;

the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), and the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitā*). Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this realm remains constant—namely, the realm of phenomena—which leads to non-forgetfulness and non-decline.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he practices for the sake of awakening to the truths; yet, the truths are not to be awakened to.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"But how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, practice for the sake of awakening to the truths? How, by so practicing, does he awaken to the truths; and having awakened to them, how does he penetrate suchness? Thus [he asked].
"By realizing this, he does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka, nor does he fall into the level of a pratyekabuddha; he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive those dharmas in such a manner..."

He sees. Seeing thus, he might apprehend some phenomenon; however, not apprehending any phenomena, he sees that all phenomena are empty. He sees that all those phenomena—both those included within the truths and those not included within the truths—are empty.
Seeing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva has entered into the fixed course (niyāma) on the stage of the lineage of the bodhisattvas.

He remains established. Having stood upon the stage of the lineage of the bodhisattvas (*bodhisattvagotrabhūmi*), he does not fall from his summit. By that falling from the summit, one would fall onto the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. Having stood here upon this stage of the lineage of the bodhisattvas, he produces the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four...

the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). Abiding here on the stage of calm (*śamatha*), he thoroughly investigates all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) and realizes the four noble truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*). He fully understands suffering (*duḥkha*), yet he does not give rise to a mind that takes suffering as its object (*ālambana*). He abandons the origin (*samudaya*), yet he does not give rise to a mind that takes the origin as its object. [He realizes] cessation (*nirodha*)...

And he realizes it, yet he does not give rise to a mind that takes cessation as its object. He cultivates the path, yet he does not give rise to a mind that takes the path as its object. Rather, with a mind inclined toward awakening, he perceives all phenomena as they truly are.
He asked: "Blessed One, what is the true nature of all phenomena?"
The Blessed One said: "Emptiness.
He asked: "What is emptiness? The Blessed One said:

[This is] the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). Through this kind of insight (*vipaśyanā*), he perceives all phenomena as empty. He does not perceive the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of any phenomenon whatsoever, wherein he might abide and fully awaken to enlightenment.
He said: "If that is so, Blessed One, is enlightenment then non-existence?"
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is, just as you say. Awakening is a non-entity; it was not made by Buddhas, nor by Pratyekabuddhas, nor by Arhats, nor even by those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas."

Those who here practice for the sake of awakening— yet other beings neither know nor see things as they truly are— the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, teaches the Dharma to those beings through skillful means. (Chapter 80)
(VIII 5,22) Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"If, Blessed One, all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature,
they were not made by Buddhas, nor by Pratyekabuddhas, nor by Arhats, nor by Anāgāmins, nor by Sakṛdāgāmins."

It was not made by stream-enterers, nor by those practicing the path, nor even by those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice here for the sake of awakening. How, then, can a differentiation or a formal establishment of these phenomena be perceived—
namely, "these are hell-beings," "these are animals," "these are inhabitants of the world of Yama," "these are gods," or "these are humans"?

By this karma there are the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama; by this karma there are the gods; by this karma there are humans; by this karma there are the gods of the Brahma-realm, up to the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
By this karma there are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas; by this karma...

By this action, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. For, Blessed One, there is no activity whatsoever belonging to non-existence by which one might go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama, or to the states of gods or humans, or even be reborn among the gods in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. [This applies to] the fruit of stream-entry...
Or whether one might attain the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or pratyekabuddhahood;

or whether a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course on the path to awakening, or a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha should attain the knowledge of all aspects— having attained which, the Blessed One said that beings [are liberated] from saṃsāra:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is, just as you say.

For, Subhūti, that which is non-existent has no action, no activity, and no fruit. For, Subhūti, the foolish, unlearned worldling, unskilled in the noble dharmas, does not understand that dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature."

With a mind arisen from perversion, he performs various kinds of karma. For him, a corresponding personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is produced—whether in the hells, or in the animal realm, or in the world of Yama, or even among the gods up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. As long as there is existence, there is no absence of karma, no absence of action, and no absence of performance.

As for the fruit: that which is non-existence is indeed non-existence. Furthermore, as Subhūti has said: "For there is no activity whatsoever belonging to non-existence by which one might attain the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship, or even pratyekabuddhahood."

"A bodhisattva or mahāsattva might practice in the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha might attain the knowledge of all aspects—having attained which he would liberate beings from saṃsāra. What do you think, Subhūti? Is the path non-existence? Is the fruit of stream-entry non-existence? Is the fruit of once-returning non-existence?"
Non-existence is the fruit of the non-returner; non-existence is arhatship; non-existence is pratyekabuddhahood; and non-existence extends even to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

He said: "O Blessed One, the path is non-existence; the fruit of stream-entry is non-existence; the fruit of once-returning is non-existence; the fruit of non-returning is non-existence; arhatship is non-existence; pratyekabuddhahood is non-existence; and non-existence extends even to the knowledge of all aspects."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti, does a non-existent phenomenon attain a non-existent phenomenon?
He replied: "No, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "It is thus, Subhūti. That which is non-existence and that which is the path—both these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, [the absence of characteristics].
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful means, [establishes] sentient beings..."

Attached to the five aggregates by means of the four perversions— perceiving the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure— he detaches them from those very entities to which they are attached. (VIII 5,23) Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

“Does there exist, Blessed One, a real thing, an existent, suchness, non-falsity, wherein foolish ordinary people abide and cling to it as a ‘thing’? Is there not a real thing, an existent, suchness, and non-falsity? If it does not exist, how do they perform karma by which karma they are not liberated from the saṃsāra of the five destinies?”
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, there is not even a thing as small as the tip of a hair that exists wherein foolish common people, abiding, perform karmic formations, except through perversion. Therefore, Subhūti, I shall give you a simile."
Thus, for the sake of further fulfilling this very point so that the wise may understand it, what do you think, Subhūti:

does there exist any real thing belonging to one who sees a dream, wherein that dreamer might dwell and enjoy himself with the five strands of sensual pleasure? He replied: "The dream itself does not even exist; how much less, then, can there be a dreamer?"
Remaining there, one should enjoy oneself with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there any dharma—whether conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows—that is not like a dream?"
He replied: "No, Blessed One. There is no phenomenon—whether conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows—that is not like a dream.
The Blessed One said:
"But is there, then, in a dream, a cyclic existence consisting of the five destinies?"
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there cultivation of the path in a dream?"
"Is there a cultivation of the path by relying upon which one would neither become defiled nor purified?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
That dharma, Blessed One, is without a basis, it is non-designatable, and it cannot be designated by any words, phrases, or syllables."
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? When a reflection is seen in the surface of a mirror, does that reflection have any substantial reality by which it could perform a karmic formation, and having performed that karmic formation, go to hell or to the animal realm?"
"Or the world of Yama, or gods and humans?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
A reflected image, Blessed One, is without substance; it is nothing other than a deception for the foolish."
How, then, could there be any karma for him—
by performing which karma he might go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama, or among gods and humans?
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Does that reflection have any cultivation of the path, by means of which cultivation of the path it would neither become defiled nor purified? Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. Since, Blessed One, that reflection is without a real basis (*avastuka*), how could there be for it any cultivation of the path, by means of which cultivation of the path it would neither become defiled... The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Regarding that echo which issues forth from a forest thicket, a mountain, a cave, or a precipice—does that echo have any substantial entity (*vastu*) that could perform an action, such that by performing that action it would go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. That echo, Blessed One, is without a substantial entity. How could there be an action belonging to it?"
Whatever karma one might perform that would lead to rebirth in hell, or in the animal realm, or in the world of Yama, or among gods and humans,
or even as far as rebirth among the gods in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
the Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Does that echo have any cultivation of the path, by means of which cultivation of the path it would neither become defiled nor purified? He replied: "Blessed One, since that echo itself does not exist in an ultimate sense, how could there be a cultivation of the path for it, by means of which cultivation of the path it would neither become defiled nor [purified]?"
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Regarding this perception of water in a mirage where there is no water, the perception of a river where there is no river, the perception of a city where there is no city, and the perception of a park where there is no park—does any karma exist within that perception of a mirage?"

Is there any karma that, having been performed, would cause one to go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama, or to be reborn among gods or humans, or even to be reborn among the gods in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
He replied: "Ultimately, Blessed One, there is no water in a mirage; nor is there a river."
There is no city or garden other than the delusion of the eye, which is a perversion of perception. How could there be any action for it?

Having performed what action would one go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama, or be reborn among gods or humans, or even be reborn among the gods in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Does that perverted perception have any cultivation of the path? Is there a cultivation of the path by relying upon which one would neither be defiled nor purified?
Subhūti replied: "No, Blessed One. A perverted perception has no cultivation of the path. There is no cultivation of the path by relying upon which one would neither be defiled nor purified."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Regarding the various magical illusions that a magician produces—whether it be a body of elephants,"
Whether it be a body of horses, or a body of oxen, or a body of infantry, or a body of chariots, or a body of women, or a body of men—
does that illusion have any real substance which, having performed an action, would go to hell or to the animal realm?
or the world of Yama, or among gods or humans, up to being reborn among the gods in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
For that illusion has no substance whatsoever, not even enough to occupy the tip of a hair-split. Where could it abide?

One would perform a formative action (karmābhisaṃskuryāt). Having performed such a formative action, one might go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama, or be reborn among gods or humans, up to being reborn among the gods in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there any cultivation of the path for that illusion, by means of which cultivation of the path one would neither be afflicted nor purified? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. How could there be a cultivation of the path for a phenomenon that lacks any real basis (avastuka)? How could there be either affliction or purification? The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? Does that emanation created by the Tathāgata have any real entity, such that by performing an action he would go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama, or be reborn among gods or humans, or even be reborn among the gods in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One; that emanation, Blessed One, is without a real basis.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does that emanation have any cultivation of the path, by means of which cultivation of the path it would neither become afflicted nor purified?"
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti, is there anyone here who is afflicted or purified?"
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, just as there is no one who is defiled and no one who is purified, even so there is neither defilement nor purification. For what reason?"

Abiding in the notions of "I" and "mine," sentient beings are either afflicted or purified; yet one who sees reality as it is is neither afflicted nor purified. Just as one who sees reality as it is is neither afflicted nor purified, even so there is neither affliction nor purification. (80)
(AdSPG II 126) Chapter 81.
(VIII 5,24) Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

O Blessed One, one who perceives reality is neither defiled nor purified; even one who does not perceive reality is neither defiled nor purified. For all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And, O Blessed One, for that which is non-existent, there is neither defilement nor purification. O Blessed One, for existence (*bhāva*) also, there is neither defilement nor purification;

for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) also, O Blessed One, there is neither defilement nor purification; and for that which has non-existence as its intrinsic nature, O Blessed One, there is neither defilement nor purification. Therefore, that which is called "purification" by the Blessed One—
"How is this so, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
"That which is the equality of all these phenomena—that, I have called purification."
He asked: "Furthermore, what is this equality of all phenomena?
The Blessed One replied:
"It is suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the nature of phenomena, the realm of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the fixed order of phenomena."

The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise—is that very stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Subhūti, this is purification;
yet it is expressed by way of worldly convention. Furthermore, it is inexpressible and beyond verbalization, transcending all paths of speech, sound, and language.

( VIII 5,25) He said: "If, Blessed One, all dharmas are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a magical creation, then how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, amidst all dharmas that are like dreams, like echoes, like reflections, like mirages, like illusions— dharmas that are without substance and without reality— [strive] for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
He generates the thought: "I shall fulfill the perfection of generosity; I shall fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline;

I shall fulfill the perfection of patience; I shall fulfill the perfection of vigor; I shall fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration; I shall fulfill the perfection of supernormal knowledges; [and] the four meditative absorptions and the four immeasurables."

The four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the noble eightfold path, the three gateways to liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the gateways of retention, and the gateways of meditative concentration.

Up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and the eighty secondary characteristics (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*), he brings to perfection a great radiance which pervades the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system with its light;

he brings to perfection the voice of Brahmā, by which, with a single sound, having understood the mental deliberations of beings in the world systems of the ten directions through their very minds according to their inclinations—
"I shall teach the Dharma.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Are these dharmas not like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a magical creation, as you have described them?"

He said: "Blessed One, if these dharmas are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a magical creation, then how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom?
For, Blessed One, a dream is not real, nor indeed is anything up to a magical creation. Indeed, Blessed One, it is not possible by means of what is unreal to [practice] the perfection of giving."

"By practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom— up to practicing the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— one is able to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. For it is not possible for one who courses in what is unreal to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening while coursing in the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom—up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. All these..."
Dharmas are conditioned and volitionally produced. Indeed, it is not possible to attain all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) by means of dharmas that are conditioned and volitionally produced.
Furthermore, Subhūti, all these dharmas lead to the bringing forth of the path and to the arising of the path, but they do not lead to the realization of the fruit.

That which is the non-arising and non-manifestation of these phenomena is also without characteristics. Therefore, from the first production of the thought of awakening until that very same point, the bodhisattva mahāsattva undertakes those very wholesome qualities— whether it be the perfection of generosity, or the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of patience, or the perfection of vigor, or the perfection of meditative concentration.

Whether it be the perfection of wisdom, or the meditative concentrations, or the immeasurables, or the formless attainments, or the foundations of mindfulness up to the path; whether it be internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
or the liberations, the nine successive attainments, or even the unique qualities of a Buddha—all that.

He knows that all things have the nature of an illusion. It is not possible, without fulfilling these dharmas—the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—to bring sentient beings to maturity. Therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] in the perfection of wisdom...

Whatever wholesome dharma he undertakes while practicing, he knows it all to be like a dream; indeed, he knows it to be like a magical creation (*nirmitopama*). Practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he knows everything up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) to be like a dream; indeed, he knows it to be like a magical creation. He knows that all those sentient beings move about in a dream, and so on, until they move about in a magical creation.

Thus he knows. Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, he apprehends phenomena as being like a dream from the standpoint of their non-existence; having so apprehended them, he eventually attains all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Likewise, he apprehends phenomena as being like a magical creation from the standpoint of their non-existence; having so apprehended them, he eventually attains all-aspect omniscience. And the perfection of wisdom is itself ungraspable.

Up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), they are ungraspable. Having realized that all phenomena are ungraspable, the bodhisattva mahāsattva aspires for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are indeed ungraspable, devoid of substantiality, and like a dream, up to being like a magical creation.
Nor can an ungraspable dharma attain an ungraspable dharma;
it is only that sentient beings do not know and do not see these dharmas.
Therefore, for the sake of all sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes himself in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
And from the first production of the thought of enlightenment onward, whatever gift he gives, that is for the sake of all sentient beings;

whatever ethical discipline he maintains, whatever patience he cultivates, whatever vigor he exerts, whatever meditative concentration he enters, and whatever wisdom he cultivates, that is for the sake of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, it is not for his own sake, nor does the bodhisattva mahāsattva establish himself in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of anyone else other than for the sake of all sentient beings;

while practicing the perfection of wisdom, he [regards] those who abide with the perception of a "sentient being" where there is no sentient being, and with the perception of a "self" where there is no self.

Thus they remain fixed upon the notions of a living being (*jantu*), a man (*manuja*), a human (*mānava*), a person (*poṣa*), an individual (*pudgala*), an agent (*kāraka*), one who causes another to act (*kārāpaka*), an instigator (*samutthāpaka*), and an experiencer (*vedaka*) or one who causes another to experience (*vedayitrī*).

Even unto those who do not know, they remain fixed with the notion that they know; those who do not see, they remain fixed with the notion that they see. He causes them to separate from these perversions (*viparyāsa*). Having separated them from perversion, he establishes them in the deathless realm (*amṛta-dhātu*), wherein for those established, [there is no further falling back].
These modes of conduct do not arise—neither the perception of a self, nor even the perception of an agent or one who causes another to act.

Having abandoned all these flickerings, imaginings, stirrings, and conceptual proliferations, he dwells having frequently attained a state of mind that is free from such imaginings. Subhūti, it is by this skillful means that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [courses] in the perfection of wisdom.
While practicing, he himself does not become attached to any dharma whatsoever; nor does he establish all sentient beings in non-attachment.
This is according to worldly convention, and not, however, according to the ultimate truth.
He said: "O Blessed One, as for that dharma which has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata..."
"Furthermore, was he awakened through worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*), or through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?

The Blessed One said: "It is expressed by means of worldly convention, saying: 'This Dharma has been awakened to by the Tathāgata. Yet, herein nothing at all is found; this Dharma has not been awakened to by means of that Dharma."
Why is that?

Because this is indeed a form of apprehension, namely: "By means of this dharma, this dharma has been fully awakened to. And by means of duality, there is no attainment whatsoever, nor is there any realization.
He said: "If, Blessed One, there is neither attainment nor realization by means of duality,"
"But is attainment and clear realization through non-duality?
The Blessed One said:
"There is no attainment and no clear realization through duality, nor is there attainment and clear realization through non-duality."
Just as here there is both attainment and clear realization, yet therein there is neither duality nor non-duality. For what reason?

Because this "attainment" and this "clear realization" are mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). And in the sameness of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*), there is no conceptual proliferation; for the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is free from conceptual proliferation.
He asked: "Blessed One, for all phenomena which have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, what is the equality of phenomena?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this very context, the equality of phenomena is that wherein there is neither existence nor non-existence, neither intrinsic nature nor verbal proclamation."
The sameness of phenomena is not proclaimed,
nor is any other phenomenon apprehended within the sameness of phenomena. With the exception of the sameness of phenomena—
which transcends all phenomena— the sameness of phenomena is neither an object of approach nor an object of domain for anyone, whether a fool or a noble one.
He asked: "But, Blessed One, is the sameness of phenomena (dharmasamatā) even beyond the range of the Tathāgata?
The Blessed One replied:

"It is beyond the range, Subhūti—the sameness of phenomena is beyond the range of all noble ones (ārya), whether they be stream-enterers (srotāpanna), once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returners (anāgāmin), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas."
[This] is even beyond the range of a Tathāgata.
He asked: "But, Blessed One, does not the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, have mastery over the range of all dharmas?
The Blessed One said:

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, would not be a master with sovereign power over the domain of all phenomena if the sameness of phenomena were one thing and the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha were another; for, Subhūti,
that which is the sameness of phenomena of ordinary persons, that which is the sameness of phenomena of stream-enterers, and that which is the sameness of phenomena of once-returners— [are all one].
The equality of phenomena belonging to non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas is a single equality;
and within that equality, there is no distinction whatsoever.
The equality of ordinary persons and the equality of all noble ones are one single equality;
in that single equality there is no duality, such as "this is an ordinary person" or "this is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. All these phenomena are not apprehended within equality.
He said: "Bhagavān, if all these phenomena are not apprehended within the equality of all phenomena, then this ordinary person..."

"This one is a stream-enterer, this one is a once-returner, this one is a non-returner, this one is an arhat, this one is a pratyekabuddha, this one is a bodhisattva, and this one is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha. If it were so, there would be no distinction between ordinary persons and stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas.
[This applies] to the Bodhisattvas and to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. There is no distinction in the equality of all dharmas."
[This applies] from ordinary worldlings up to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

He asked: "Blessed One, if there is no distinction between ordinary worldlings and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, then, Blessed One, from where does the manifestation of these three jewels in the world arise—the jewel of the Buddha, the jewel of the Dharma, and the jewel of the Saṅgha?"
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the jewel of the Buddha one thing, the jewel of the Dharma another, the jewel of the Saṅgha another, and the sameness of phenomena yet another?
He replied: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, the jewel of the Buddha is not one thing and the jewel of the Dharma another."

The Jewel of the Saṅgha is one thing, and the sameness of phenomena (dharmasamatā) is another. Blessed One, that which is the Jewel of the Buddha, that which is the Jewel of the Dharma, and that which is the Jewel of the Saṅgha—all these are precisely the sameness of phenomena.

All these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Blessed One, how does one establish the distinction among these phenomena that are without characteristics— such as: "this is an ordinary person," "this is a stream-enterer," "this is a once-returner," "this is a non-returner," "this is an arhat," "this is a pratyekabuddha," "this is a bodhisattva," and "this is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha"?
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. This is the domain of the Tathāgata; this is the personal achievement of the Tathāgata, namely, the establishment of dharmas that are without characteristics."

He performs it. What do you think, Subhūti: if the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha had not awakened to enlightenment, and if, without having awakened to it, he had not established the classification of phenomena, would hell be known, or the animal realm, or the world of Yama? Or would gods or humans be known, or the Cāturmahārājakāyika [gods]?

Or up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, or the Brahmakāyika gods, or up to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; or the foundations of mindfulness, up to the noble eightfold path, the three gateways to liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, and so forth...
"Will the emptiness of specific characteristics, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, be cognized?
He replied: "They will not be cognized, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Subhūti, this is the *puruṣakāra* (heroic effort) of the Tathāgata: that he does not waver from the sameness of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*) and yet establishes the differentiation of phenomena. Subhūti asked: "But, Blessed One, is it just as the Tathāgata does not waver from the sameness of phenomena, so too [does he establish their differentiation]?"

Ordinary worldlings do not waver. Likewise, stream-enterers do not waver. Likewise, up to and including pratyekabuddhas, they do not waver. Likewise, up to and including bodhisattvas, they do not waver.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. All phenomena, Subhūti, do not move from the equality of phenomena (dharmasamatā), nor do they deviate. Why is that?

That which is the suchness (tathatā) of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—their non-falsity, their non-other-suchness, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthititā), the fixed order of phenomena (dharma-niyāmatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)—that very same suchness, up to the limit of reality, is the suchness of foolish ordinary people."

That very suchness of those who follow through faith, those who follow through dharma, the eighth-rank practitioners, stream-enterers, up to the bodhisattvas, the great beings, extends as far as the limit of reality. All these dharmas do not transcend the sameness of dharmas. Why is that?
Because the suchness of those [practitioners], up to the limit of reality, is not other than the sameness of dharmas.

He said: "If, Blessed One, that very same equality of phenomena (dharmasamatā) which belongs to ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) is also the same for stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, and is that very same equality of phenomena for Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas,"
"O Blessed One, these phenomena are characterized by distinct natures; namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The true nature of form is one thing, that of feeling another, that of perception another, that of mental formations another, and that of consciousness another. Furthermore, the true nature of the eye is one thing, that of the ear another, that of the nose another, that of the tongue another, that of the body another, and that of the mind another."

The nature of the earth element is one thing, the water element another, the fire element another, the wind element another, the space element another, and the consciousness element another; the true nature of passion is one thing, that of hatred another, that of delusion another, that of the views held by others another, that of the meditative absorptions another, that of the immeasurables another, that of the formless attainments another, and that of the foundations of mindfulness another.

...up to: is the noble eightfold path one thing, emptiness another, signlessness another, wishlessness another, internal emptiness another, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature another; are the liberations one thing, the serial attainments another, the powers another, the grounds of self-confidence another, the analytical knowledges another, great loving-kindness another, and great compassion another?

The true nature (*dharmatā*) of the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) is one thing; the true nature of the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) is another; the true nature of the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*) is yet another.
Lord, how can the true nature of such diverse phenomena be of a single characteristic?
How, then, does the systematic arrangement of phenomena occur?
Establishing what does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, differentiate between phenomena?
For it is not possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to practice the perfection of wisdom without differentiating between phenomena.

And how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, pass from stage to stage and enter the state of certainty (*nyāma*)? By means of that entry into certainty, he transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Having transcended them, he fulfills the superknowledges (*abhijñā*). Sporting with those superknowledges, he fulfills the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
He fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration;

sporting, he travels from buddhafield to buddhafield, attending upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and plants roots of merit therein. By means of those roots of merit, he brings all sentient beings to maturity and takes hold of a buddhafield.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"Furthermore, as for what Subhūti has said: 'If the very sameness of all dharmas is the same as the sameness of dharmas of ordinary persons, and the same as the sameness of dharmas of stream-enterers, up to the same as the sameness of dharmas of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas...'"
The sameness of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*). How is it logical that the sameness of phenomena—which are characterized by diverse marks—is of a single mark?
What do you think, Subhūti? Is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of form not indeed emptiness itself? Is the true nature of the Tathāgatas not indeed emptiness itself?
He replied: "It is indeed emptiness, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? In emptiness, are any distinct characteristics found—namely, the distinct characteristic of form, of feeling, of perception, of volitional formations, of consciousness, and so on, up to the characteristic of a Tathāgata?"
He said: “No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

“Therefore, Subhūti, by this method you should understand it thus: that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, therein there is neither an ordinary person nor anything other than an ordinary person; up to and including, therein there is neither a Tathāgata nor anything other than a Tathāgata.”
( VIII 5,26) He asked: "Is this *dharmatā* conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
The Blessed One said: "It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned."
Furthermore, the unconditioned is not found apart from the conditioned, nor is the conditioned perceived apart from the unconditioned. Thus, Subhūti,
that which is the conditioned realm and that which is the unconditioned realm— both these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined.
They are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being characterless;

yet the Tathāgata expresses this by means of worldly convention, not by means of the ultimate truth. Furthermore, in the ultimate truth, there is no formation of body, nor formation of speech, nor formation of mind. Nor is there anything other than these formations of body.

The ultimate reality is not found apart from the formations of speech, nor apart from the formations of mind. That which is the equality of these phenomena—both conditioned and unconditioned—is the ultimate reality.
Thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, he does not deviate from the ultimate reality, yet he performs the work of a bodhisattva.
Chapter 82. Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"If, Blessed One, the sameness of all dharmas is empty by nature,..."

Therefore, he does nothing at all to any phenomenon. How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom among phenomena that are either non-existent or devoid of anything, does not deviate from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and yet performs the work for the sake of all sentient beings through generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful action, and consistency of purpose?
The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti; so it is, just as you have spoken. That which is emptiness does nothing to anyone, nor does it do nothing at all. If, Subhūti, those beings were to know emptiness by themselves, this would not be the task of the Tathāgata."

Therein lies the bull-like power (*vṛṣabhitā*) of a Tathāgata: that he does not waver from emptiness, yet he detaches sentient beings from the notion of a self; having detached them, he liberates them from cyclic existence through emptiness. In this same way, [he detaches them] from the notion of a being, up to the notion of an agent;
from the notion of form, up to the notion of consciousness; from the notion of the eye, up to the notion of the mind; and from the notion of the earth element.

He discriminates from the perception of the element of consciousness up to the perception of the conditioned element. Having discriminated them, he establishes them in the unconditioned element; and that unconditioned element is empty.
(VIII 5,27) He asked: "By what is it empty?
The Blessed One replied:
"It is empty of all conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*). Furthermore, Subhūti, if a created being were to create another created being, would there be any entity whatsoever therein that is not emptiness?"

He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One, for that which is an emanation has no entity whatsoever that is not emptiness. That which is emptiness and that which is an emanation—both these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined;
both are empty of emptiness. Why then should one conceal this, thinking 'this is emptiness' and 'this is an emanation'? For what reason?"
Nevertheless, both of these—“this is emptiness” and “this is a magical creation”—are not apprehended within emptiness.
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, there is no form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness, up to and including that which is a magical creation; for there is nothing that is not a magical creation."

He said: "If, Blessed One, these worldly dharmas are emanations, are then these supramundane dharmas also emanations— namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the three gates of liberation, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?"

And as for their fruit, by which those persons are designated— namely, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha— are these dharmas indeed emanations? The Blessed One said:

Furthermore, Subhūti, since all phenomena are emanations— in which some are emanations of śrāvakas, some are emanations of pratyekabuddhas, some are emanations of bodhisattvas, some are emanations of Tathāgatas, some are emanations of afflictions, and some are emanations of karma— [how could there be any grasping?]

"In this manner, Subhūti, all phenomena are like magical illusions. He asked: "Furthermore, Blessed One, regarding this abandonment—the fruit of stream-entry up to arhatship—are these phenomena also magical illusions?"
Whether it be the stage of a Pratyekabuddha or the stage of a Buddha, there is the abandonment of all habitual tendencies and their continuations. Are these dharmas, moreover, emanated?
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, some dharmas..."
Whether they have been produced or ceased, all of them are emanations.
He asked: "Blessed One, what is the dharma that is not an emanation?"
The Blessed One said:
"He for whom there is neither arising nor cessation is not a created being.
He asked: "Who, then, is he?"
The Blessed One said:
"The Dharma, which has the nature of never being lost and is coextensive with Nirvāṇa, is not a creation.

He asked: "Furthermore, Blessed One, it was said by the Blessed One that one does not deviate from emptiness; it is not apprehended as a duality, and there is no dharma whatsoever that is not emptiness. Therefore, Blessed One, [is] the Nirvāṇa that has the nature of never being lost..."
"It will be a creation.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Subhūti, all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature;
they were not made by śrāvakas, nor by pratyekabuddhas, nor by bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, nor by tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened ones.
And that which is the emptiness of specific characteristics—that is nirvāṇa.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, how should a beginner person be instructed and how should they be exhorted so that they may understand the emptiness of intrinsic nature?
The Blessed One said:

Furthermore, Subhūti, how could it be that what was previously an entity will later become a non-entity? Here, Subhūti, there is neither entity nor non-entity, neither intrinsic nature nor extrinsic nature. How much less, then, can there be the emptiness of intrinsic nature? The eighty-second chapter, "The Exposition of the Immovable Nature of Phenomena," in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, is completed.
